maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. I would like to bring to the attention of the government certain remarks of the Solicitor General (Mr. Lemi-eux) as reported in the press despatches. The Solicitor General seems to have undertaken to give information to the British public with regard to more than one matter. The first subject is the attitude of this country respecting preferential trade. The history of that movement in this country and in Great Britain is pretty well known. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Lauder) adopted it as part of his platform in 1890. He declared himself as much in favour of inter-imperial preferential trade as was Sir Charles Tupper, and promised to do everything he could to obtain it. In 1897, a preference was granted as a measure of free trade and as a compromise between the warring factions of the government. The right hon. Prime Minister went to Great Britain and told the people there that Canada wanted no preference in return for the preference we had granted, that our action was in return for the splendid freedom which Great Britain had given us. And he further said that he did not want Great Britain cursed with the protection which has wrought so much evil in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) repeated the same observations in 1901 on at least two occasions. At the Colonial Conference in 1902, this government practically threatened the government of Great Britain with the withdrawal of the preference unless some preference was given in return. No meaning could be placed on the language except that. It was not language used casually, but was contained in a carefully-prepared memorandum. So, it became apparent that the views that the right hon. gentleman had expressed in 1897, and that had been repeated by the Minister of Agriculture in 1901. had ceased to occupy the minds of this government, and that their intentions pointed in the very opposite direction. In 1903 and during the present year there has been a movement led by

Mr. Chamberlain in Great Britain. Tliat movement has attracted great attention not only in the mother country blit throughout the empire. It has beeu asserted against Mr. Chamberlain, that Canada was taking no interest in that movement, and it has been pointed out that, while only one or two provinces of the Dominion and certain boards of trade had adopted resolutions favouring Mr. Chamberlain's policy, the parliament of Canada had given no sign-had expressed no opinion whatever, upon the advantages or disadvantages of his policy.
The excuse, the reason for this, put forward in government organs-and I believe it is no secret that the right hon. gentleman shared that opinion-was that this being a matter of political controversy in the United Kingdom between those who favoured Mr. Chamberlain's policy and those who were opposed to it, it *would be unbecoming and in bad taste for this parliament to express any opinion upon the subject. That view was voiced by the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in his speech upon the budget last year, w'lhen he said in so many words that it would be unbecoming for parliament to take any part in the movement by signifying the willingness or unwillingness of Canada to adopt a policy such as that which Sir. Chamberlain was advocating ; although it is a policy, so far as its essentia] features and its principle are concerned, which bad been adopted by both parties in this country in the election campaign of 1896. Well, if that were a good reason why the parliament of Canada should refrain from expressing any opinion upon the subject, it seems to me that it is a much stronger reason wliy a member of this government, visiting the United Kingdom on official business of this country, should not attend partisan meetings in the mother country and express himself as either opposed to or in favour of Mr. Chamberlain's policy. That hon. gentleman's remarks are thus reported in a cable from London, under date July 18 :
Surprise is expressed at the speech delivered by Mr. Rodolphe Lemieux, the Solicitor-General for Canada, at a Liberal demonstration at Dollis Hill House on Saturday. After remarking that Canadians were following the fiscal discussion very closely, Mr. Lemieux said they should apply to the present position between the Colonies and the Empire, the old axiom,
' Let well alone.' He added that Canadians were loyal, happy and satisfied to live under the British flag, but if they wished to tighten the tie, they would break it.
The anti-Chamberlainite papers are making use of this statement, the inference made being that a section of the Canadian Cabinet is opposed to the preferential policy despite Mr. Fielding's declaration in the budget speech. This is regarded specially unfortunate on the eve of the publication of the report of the tariff commission, which is expected to base the whole Chamberlainite policy emphatically upon closer Anglo-Colonial trade relations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I may say that I do not regard the language of Mr. Lemieux in dealing with the tie which binds the mother country to the colonies as especially happy. The suggestion that a very slight movement might break the tie between the mother country and the colonies is one which I think will not be appreciated by the majority of the people of Canada, and is one as to which I do not think Mr. Lemieux speaks for the majority of the people of Canada, if be desired to suggest any such condition of public opinion as existing in Canada at the present time. We have another report, under date July 19. But I may say before coming to that that the language of the Solicitor General to-dav is in marked contrast to that of tlie Prime Minister himself when in Great Britain some years ago, because on that occasion, if I remember rightly-I do not presume to quote his exact words-he said that whenever the beacon fires were lighted on the hill-tops, Canadians would rally to the support of the empire, or words to that effect. The report under date July 19 is as follows :
Fuller reports of the political demonstration, at which Hon. R. Lemieux spoke on Saturday, show its bitterly partisan character. One speaker spoke of the downward path that had led Mr. Chamberlain to his present condition of the most reactionary figure in politics. Another declared it would take the whole time of the next Radical Parliament to undo the misdeeds of the Balfour Ministry.
Mr. Lemieux declared that Canada asked nothing in return for the preference, and was ready to continue it without asking anything in return, because Canadians were not going to put their loyalty up for sale. He added that they should apply to the present position between the Colonies and the Empire the old maxim, * let well alone.'
Mr. Lemieux was perfectly correct in that part of his remarks wherein he spates that Canadians are not going to put their loyalty up for sale, but it is to be borne in mind that we have always been told by the present administration that in dealing with commercial matters, with trade relations between the mother country and the colonies, the mother country was absolutely devoid of sentiment and would deal with us purely on business principles. We do not propose in Canada to put our loyalty up for sale, but we do profess, or at least some of us have professed to believe, that a policy by which mutual preferences would be granted by the mother country on the one hand and the colonies on the other hand would be of great importance indeed, not only commercially, but as a means of solidifying and uniting the* empire.
I would also like to call attention to Mr. Lemieux's remarks on another occasion, to a cable despatch in which he is reported to have said :
Unless the British government recalls Lord Dundonald immediately the bitterest feelings

will be aroused in Canada against the imperial military authorities.
Well, I doubt very much if the hon. Solicitor General has any mandate from the people of Canada to express that opinion. He on this occasion also said :
The ' Times' is always against the Laurier government. It gives Lord Dundonald's version ' of the case completely ignoring the government side. There is no doubt but that Lord Dundonald is now playing into the hands of the Canadian opposition in view of the coming elections. The meeting held in Toronto was nothing else but a pretext tc arouse the feelings of Ontario against Sir Wilfrid. Laurier, but rest assured there is enough common sense in Canada to understand the true position.

speechtext: He told the truth then.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I am very glad to have the endorsation of that remark by the Postmaster General. Another gentleman. I think, in the British House of Commons said that the opposition were endeavouring to exploit Lord Dundonald. '

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: My hon. friend the Postmaster General endorses that remark also V

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I do.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: All I have to sa'y is that if there is any reason for making that statement I am not aware of it. Perhaps the Postmaster General, if he conies to address the House, will be good enough to state the facts upon which he grounds that expression of opinion for which he, as a cabinet minister of this country, ought to be held responsible. I say that the Con servative party has not endeavoured to exploit Lord Dundonald, and has not-

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: And has not had anything to do, so far as I am aware, with any reception which has been tendered to him on any occasion. I say that, speaking upon my responsibility as leader in this House of the Conservative party, and as knowing something of that party's affairs. I say further, that the opposition in this House have a perfect right to criticise the action of the government in connection "with the administration of the militia, and, therefore, in connection with the circumstances which led up to the dismissal of Lord Dundonald. If that is exploiting Lord Dundonald, they have a perfect right to exploit him. If by the expression ' exploiting Lord Dundonald ' anything more than that is meant, then I say that those who make that charge, and especially the Postmaster General, who has not been, afraid to endorse it, as he calls it, in this House, ought to state the facts on which they rely when making any such statement. Lord Dundonald has been exploited, has he ? When the circumstances of his dismissal were brought up in this House, was it not in order for the opposition to call attention to and discuss the facts connected with the administration of the militia which had been stated in his speech in Montreal, and which were practically admitted by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), as well as1 by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) ? Were their mouths to be shut, and are they to be precluded in any way from discussing various matters connected with the Militia Department, of which Lord Dundonald has spoken since his dismissal ? For what is an opposition In parliament, if not to discuss matters of this kind ? I do not understand the suggestion of the hon. Postmaster General.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: We are not here to make incendiary speeches.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Who ?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General

speechtext: Hon. gentlemen.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Who is not ?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: No one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is referring to himself or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I refer to any one who makes incendiary speeches in this House or out of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's observations are of a remarkably general and vague nature. Until be comes down to the particular I will not deal further with his remarks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: He is just soliloquizing over his own misconduct in days gone by.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.

speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
As far as Lord Dundonald is concerned I am not here to defend him. He is absolutely able to defend himself but when public men in this House and in this country, such as the hon. Postmaster General, are apparently of the opinion that Lord Dundonald. since his dismissal from the position of General Officer Commanding, is bound to sit silent under the most venomous, and if his statement is to be believed, the most untruthful attacks, and not

say one word in his own defence, I say that is a position which T do not acquiesce in for one moment. The position of the hon. Postmaster General seems to be that Lord Dundonald is to be gagged and that he is to be subjected to every possible charge that can be made against him in this parliament and in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow me ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: My observations had no reference whatever to Lord Dundonald himself. My observations had reference to those gentlemen who are exploiting Lord Dundonald for their own political advantage.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
Well, I think the hon. Postmaster General's observations must particularly have reference to himself and no doubt an uneasy conscience is that which prompts such observations. If there has been any exploiting in this incident I would be able to show, if it were desirable or necessary to do so, where the exploiting has been. I will give you one illustration and more can be given. Those who enter these grounds may read the inscription which has been many months near the entrance gates :
' Lisez le Canada,' organe du Sir Wilfri Laurier.
In that paper only of yesterday's date there is a long extract, not an editorial, but a long extract from another journal published for the obvious purpose of convincing the people of Quebec that Lord Dundonald unjustly discriminated against them. I would call that exploiting this incident for political purposes. I would call that exploiting this incident for unworthy purposes more than anything that I have heard of in connections with the *whole question. A great many other illustrations of the same kind could be given. But so far as I am concerned in regard to Lord Dundonald I have taken the opportunity in this House of speaking upon the incidents which led up to his dismissal. I have not justified his remarks at Montreal as not being a breach of discipline. Lord Dundonald himself has said that he knew perfectly well what he was doing when he made these remarks and that he did it with an obvious purpose, but that did not preclude me from criticising the government in connection with the facts which led up to Lord Dundonald's dismissal and it does not in the least vary the original condition of affairs which in the judgment of Lord Dundonald made it necessary for him to speak out on that occasion. Whether he was wise or unwise, whether he was guilty of a breach of discipline or otherwise is a subject I have not discussed in this House beyond pointing out that so far as the military regula-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
tions which were invoked by the right hon. leader of the government were concerned, they could have no application to that particular incident ; otherwise, dozens of military officers throughout the country who had spoken in commendation of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence and of the administration of the militia would be equally liable with Lord Dundonald to dismissal because the regulation that was cited by the right hon. Prime Minister applied not only to terms of reprobation but applied equally to terms of commendation of a superior officer.
I think it is to be regretted that the hon. Solicitor General has taken part in a bitterly partisan gathering in the mother country and has seen fit at that gathering to discuss a subject which is a matter of political controversy in the mother country, which is so mifch a matter of political controversy in the mother country that the right hon. Prime Minister and his government have thought that we should not discuss it or deal with it by resolution in this House during the past two years.
I think it is also to be regretted that he spoke in the tone in which he did of the loyalty of Canadians, because, as far as I am concerned, I believe that the loyalty of Canadians in the province of Quebec, in the province of Ontario, and in the other provinces of Canada is made of more substantial stuff than that which would be gathered from the remarks of the hon. Solicitor General.
Right hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister). Mr. Speaker, the occasion of the speech which we have just listened to from my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is the publication of certain remarks which are attributed to my hon. friend the Solicitor General now in England upon official duties. Upon these remarks the hon. leader of the opposition has made some comments which I think are hardly justified by the occasion. I do not believe that my hon. friend or any other member of this House would consent to be tried and judged upon telegraphic extracts from reports of what he may have said in any part of the world or even in Canada. I do not believe that it would be fair to my hon. friend the Solicitor General to come to any conclusion upon the remarks which have been attributed to him and which he is said to have made in a meeting of the Liberal party in Great Britain. I have only to call the attention of the House to the fact that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has quoted two versions of the remarks which have been said to have been made by Mr. Lemieux on that occasion and that these remarks do not bear at all the same construction. One of these versions could not only be accepted without comment and without criticism but could be accepted as fairly expressing the views of

anybody. If Mr. Lemieux attended any meeting at all I do not think that of set purpose he went to any political gathering in Great Britain and until such time as we have received from Mr. Lemieux himself an authoritative version of what he said, I decline for my part to discuss the statements of Mr. Lemieux.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Is my right lion, friend under the impression that this was not a political partisan gathering ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I do not say that. Mr. Lemieux may have found himself in a political gathering-I do not know that ; but I remember on one occasion I was myself accused of having attended a certain meeting-it was the occasion of Mr. Redmond's lecture in Ottawa-when I had been there merely as a spectator and had paid for my ticket like everybody else. I did not think I had done anything to which exception could be taken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: My right hon. friend did not speak.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I did not speak, and when we know what Mr. Lemieux really said it may be that no objection can be offered to it at all. It is the fate of all of us that certain language may be attributed to us which has not been reported properly ; and, moreover, if Mr. Lemieux made a speech there it must have been a speech which would occupy some time in its delivery, but as we have it cabled it is condensed into one or two sentences, so that it would not be fair to hold Mr. Lemieux accountable on the basis of what must be a very incomplete report. The only thing which Mr. Lemieux is alleged to have said, and which has caused comment in this country, is a reference to the loyalty of Canadians. Well, Mr. Speaker, for my part I have only this to say once for all : I do not think we are called upon | to defend our loyalty on any occasion. It 1 is very much to be regretted that any Canadian should find himself called upon from time to time to defend his loyalty ; but it is unfortunate that we have to take that stand sometimes, and Mr. Lemieux may have found it advisable to defend himself and his own countrymen. We find our loyalty attacked -I will not say on the floor of this House- we find our loyalty attacked, if not openly, by way of insinuation. The newspaper press of a certain party has time and again stated that we are influenced by secret' motives when we pursue a certain line of policy as a political party. Not only that, but if one of us by a slip of the tongue utters a word which he immediately corrects, even that is supposed to betray the secret feelings of the heart. Under such circumstances, and as we are all human, allowance must be made if a man reflecting upon these facts thinks it advisable to utter certain language in defence of the loyalty of his countrymen
of his own blood, which under other conditions there should be no necessity for uttering. For my part, I should not attempt to defend Mr. Lemieux or anybody else. Our history is there to speak for itself. I agree with Mr. Lemieux that our loyalty is not for sale, and that whatever may be the attitude taken on the question of the preference it should not weigh one iota in the loyalty which we have for, and which we owe to Great Britain. I have said on previous occasions, and I have not been contradicted-I think the leader of the opposition endorsed the views I expressed a moment ago-I have said on many occasions that our commercial relations with Great Britain should be above all things based on considerations of mutual interest. When we gave the preference we gave it without any return on the part of Great Britain. We thought we were serving the interests of Canada on that occasion, and if we have to discuss the question later on, we should again decide on our course in a manner which will serve the best interests of Canada. That is all I have to say with regard to the alleged remarks attributed to ill-. Lemieux.
As to the observations Mr. Lemieux is stated to have made in an interview, even for these remarks I would not hold Mr. Lemieux accountable until he has had an opportunity of stating whether the views put in his mouth are true or not. I hold it to be a sacred principle in political and public life, not*only between party and party, but between individual and individual, that a man is not to be judged upon what he is reported to have said unless he has had an opportunity of saying : these are my words or these are not my words. If Mr. Lemieux said yesterday that Lord Dundonald ought to be recalled, I imagine he simply reflected not so much his own opinion as the opinion of the British government, expressed not later than yesterday in the British House of Commons. As to the action of Lord Dundonald, I have not a word to say. He has chosen his own course ; his course is before the public ; it is for the public to decide. As to that incident, I have said everything I want to say on the floor of this House, and unless perhaps our attitude is again challenged. I may perhaps make this remark, that whilst it is said in the Conservative press that the dismissal of Lord Dundonald has been unjust and tyrannical, the hon. the leader of the opposition is himself bound to admit that in this House he will not challenge the dismissal of Lord Dundonald. More than this I will not say upon the present occasion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
In his concluding remarks the prime minister referred to the action of the British government yesterday as reported in the press, but a moment before the right hon. gentleman condemned' the leader of the opposition for basing his remarks on a newspaper report of the speech
*7091

of the Solicitor General, which he thinks may not be correct. On what authority does the Prime Minister justify the British government for its expression of opinion yesterday ? On what authority did Mr. Arnold Foster address the House of Commons yesterday, and state in these words as' reported.
Mr. Arnold Foster (Secretary of State for War) welcomed Mr. Churchill as the spokesman of the opposition in this debate which was not calculated to contribute to the public advantage. One question was that of war office discipline, of which he was in charge, and the other was the advisability of this debate. He saw that no advantage could arise from this debate except to make bad blood between two great branches of the empire. Did Mr. Lloyd George, he asked, speak as the representative of.Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
I might here remark that it Is a strange [DOT] coincidence thht the right hon. the first minister finds himself endorsed by the disloyal men of the empire ; by Mr. Lloyd George, a pro-Boer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: And Winston Churchill.

I think it is desirable that a word or two should be said on that question. There are many matters in which the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament would naturally desire the cooperation and assistance of the government of the mother country, and in all such cases we would naturally appeal to that government for aid and assistance. But there are other matters in which no such aid is needed, and this unhappy Dundonald business was one of that kind. Mr. Arnold Foster, very

correctly stated-aud it is perhaps the point | of his observations which we appreciate most-that this is a matter in which the Canadian government have shown that they were well able to deal with the situation themselves. It was stated correctly by Mr. Arnold Foster that this government have made no protest whatever with regard to Lord Dundonald. We have not felt called upon to make any such protest. Lord Dundonald was an official of the Canadian government when he made what I regard as an unfortunate mistake, a mistake which many a brave soldier makes when he comes to deal with civil affairs. We felt that we had to deal with that question as between the Canadian government and one of its public officials. It is not to be supposed for a moment that any Canadian official, a servant of the government-I do not use the word in an offensive sense, because each one of us is a servant, using the word in its proper sense-can be permitted to go out and make public attacks upon the ministry of the day without being rebuked or dismissed. It is not necessary to discuss what had happened prior to that. It was enough to know that a servant of the government of Canada bad made the grave mistake of making an attack upon the ministers who were his superiors in power. It was necessary for the vindication of our self-respect, it was necessary for the vindication of the principles of responsible government, it was necessary for the vindication of all that Canadians have valued in their struggles for self-government, that the right of the responsible ministers of the day should be asserted, and there seemed to be no other way of asserting this right than by dismissing that eminent and distinguished officer. That being the case we did not feel it necessary to make any protest as to his further action, but nevertheless, we appreciate in the highest degree the manner in which that question was dealt with yesterday in the imperial parliament. The statement that was made in the imperial parliament that Lord Dundonald was being exploited for the benefit of a political party in this country is unhappily too true. Whatever motives Lord Dundonald may have in the matter, and I will not attempt to question his motives for a moment, we all know that gentlemen politically opposed to the government of the day have seized upon this question in the hope that they may turn it to political advantage. They have been endeavouring to beguile some Liberals into a participation in the movement, but I venture to believe that after the experience that has been had in the city of Toronto, no other example of that kind will be given. I therefore desire to say that I endorse emphatically the statement that the Dundonald question was being exploited for the advantage of a political party and that in that respect, whe-2201
ther willingly or not, Lord Dundonald was being used as an instrument in a movement not calculated to advance the best possible relations between the civil and military authorities, or between the imperial and colonial governments. While we made no representations on the subject we rejoice to know that the Secretary for War, Mr. Arnold Foster, Mr. Winston Churchill, Mr. Lloyd George, whom, notwithstanding the reference of my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes), I am bound to speak of as one of the most distinguished members of the imperial parliament, Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and all the members of parliament who spoke on this question in the great House of Commons of England recognize and appreciate the position of Canada, that they recognize that this is a purely Canadian question, that they recognize that the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament are the proper people to deal with the question, and in their intimation to Lord Dundonald, a distinguished soldier, that it was not desirable that he should participate in these party conflicts they have taken a step which again proves that the mother country can be relied upon at all times to uphold and to appreciate the principles of responsible government which we Canadians fought for many years ago.

Mr. Speaker. I am sure you cannot have failed to have observed the extraordinary nature of the logic of hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with this incident so far as the debate has [gone. The right hon. Prime Minister declined to say a word in condemnation of the Solicitor General, for the uncalled for and improper utterances he is credited with having made because the report of these utterances appears in the newspapers ; yet, when reference is made to Lord Dundonald by the newspapers based on imagination or otherwise, is there a word of protest ? This whole incident we are discussing in so far as it is connected with what has happened in the old country, is simply based on the statements of newspapers. When the newspapers say that the opposition are exploiting Lord Dundonald for the purpose of making political capital, that is sufficient in the eyes of hon. gentlemen opposite to condemn the opposition. Even *If this were a true statement of the utterances of the Solicitor General, would the right hon. Prime Minister condemn a word of them ? This question since it was first brought up. has been widened by hon. gentlemen opposite, been widened into an attack upon the Conservative party and upon the bete noir of hon. gentlemen opposite- Lord Dundonald. I was glad to observe that neither the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) nor the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) ventured to say one word in disparagement of that distinguished

soldier who was lately our commander in chief here. I was glad, because this is in marked contrast with the course pursued f>y some of ttieir associates, with some of those who sit behind them and in marked contrast with the course universally pursued by a strong element of the Reform press. They have not hesitated in any way to accuse him of everything that it is possible to imagine. Ever since what ? Ever since, with the courage of a patriot, knowing it was to his own disparagement, admitting like a soldier, a gentleman, and a Briton, that he was, prepared to pay the penalty, he felt himself impelled by his duty to speak out. Before I dwell any more upon that, let me call the attention of the bon. Minister of Finance to one thing that he did. I say that it was not worthy of him to describe Lord Dundonald as a servant of the people. It is true in one sense ; it is not true in the larger sense. He is not the servant of the people in one sense. He is no more so than the members of the government who are the representatives of the people in the higher sense and I would not think of applying that term to the hon. Minister of Finance or to any man sitting in his place because of the distinguished position he occupies in this country. He (the Minister of Finance) is more than the servant of the people; he is the representative of the people. So is Lord Dundonald. He is an official of the Canadian government, but I regretted to hear the word ' servant ' so frequently used in connection with a distinguished gentleman, always distinguished since he entered the great imperial service and a gentleman who upon his own merits during the course of his military career, has fought his way up to the exalted position he now occupies. It was not worthy of the hon. Minister of Finance to do as some of the satellites behind him have done ; that is to bring up the question of Lord Dundonald being a servant of the people so as to make the people think they had a power over this gentleman which the law of the country does not give them. Then, the hon. gentleman brought up the question of responsible government. A good point was made by one hon. gentleman opposite, this morning, one that I appreciate because I do not think it is necessary that we should be called upon in both parties to defend our loyalty as often as we are called upon to do.
I agree with the proposition that according to their light all the people in this country are loyal. But I do make this charge, and I regret it exceedingly-I am too near the end of my term of service in this country to say anything which I do not believe to be absolute reality-that gentlemen in the province of Quebec endeavour to make their compatriots believe that we in the province iof ^Ontario do not believe in their loyalty and that we are abusing and maligning them. I have stood up for the rights of my Mr. TISDALE.
French Canadian compatriots and I have paid for it by a hard political fight when I had to give a vote to preserve the constitutional rights of the people of Quebec, I say stop that, stop that the Prime Minister, stop that the Solicitor General stop it all. We in Ontario, Reformer and Conservative are as much as possible stopping it. It does not do any good and it does a great deal of harm. Why does the hon. Minister of Finance then bring up the question of responsible government 1 Why is it necessary ? We have heard more about responsible government since the Dundonald incident than it ought be necessary for us to hear in five years. No principle of constitutional government is imperilled, and if it were, Conservatives and Liberals alike, would rush to safeguard it. Let these gentlemen opposite give us some argument to show that constitutional government is in danger, and let them cease to play to the gallery and expect such nonsensical talk to he taken as argument. If I am put in possession of a single proof that the Conservative party is open to the charge of exploiting Lord Dundonald, or trying to make political capital out of the incident, I will go against my party. No, Sir, the Conservative party is too noble a party to betray the late Commander in Chief, a man who has proven himself to be a hero, and who to his own discomfort, and, when at the apex of his great career, has placed himself in at least a delicate position, in order to right the wrong. I am beginning to think, Sir, that we have been too careful in this matter and that too little has been said by us in defence of Lord Dundonald.

Hon. gentlemen opposite may laugh if they please, but I will substantiate this statement. I can tell them that their cries of militarism, constitutional government, and responsible government will not blind the good sense of the people of Canada. I have come to the conclusion that the Conservative party, in very fear of introducing politics into this, have neglected to defend Lord Dundonald us he ought to be defended for the manly part he has taken. There is no difference of opinion as to the power of the government if they saw fit to do so, to dismiss Lord Dundonald. But, Sir, there is another view of the case ; there is a larger view of the case, and that is that the people of Canada must set about to remedy the evil 'which Lord Dundonald impelled by patriotism and a high sense of duty has exposed. Is there a Reformer in Ontario who will deny that it was patriotism and a high sense of duty which impelled Lord Dundonald to the action he took. Can any other reasonable or unreasonable motive be suggested ? I can tell these gentlemen opposite that the peo-pie of this country, as distinguished from the

politicians, will appreciate the very soul of the motives which inspired Lord Dundonald. He is a reformer and he has sacrificed himself to bring about reform. Martyrs are made for the good of the Christian, as well as for the good of the political world, and I have no doubt that history will realize that for the sake of the Canadian militia Lord Dundonald lias offered himself up as a sacrifice. He is not a politician. His military and his private career show that he is an honourable and noble man. His name is a household word in the British empire and particularly in Canada since the relief of Ladysmith. Our brave young lads who God has spared from the l'isks of war, brought to their Canadian homes, honour and praise for Duudonald's name. He came here to serve the empire and his great inducement was that he might make soldiers in a simple way of the brave Canadian lads who, Conservative and Reform ,are similar to those who served under him in South Africa. A part from the politicians and apart from the party press, Lord Dundonald is honoured in Canada and his motives are correctly appreciated. And what objectionable demonstration has he taken part in since his dismissal V The first was a private dinner at the Rideau Club, which I had the honour of attending and at which there was no polities. The next was a great demonstration in the capital of my province, the centre of commerce and education, a city worthy of any country, a city that is the pride of Ontario, and the pride of myself, b cause although I was not born there, I was educated there and lived there part of my life. The citizens wanted to honour Lord Dundonald. and a committee composed of men of all political beliefs was named to entertain him and present him with au address appreciative of what he did. Thousands of Conservatives and thousands of Reformers assembled in Toronto to do Dundonald honour. They expected him to m ike his defence against the charges hurled against him, and they would have been disappointed if he had not done so. It would be too much to expect that he should keep his mouth closed. When the address was presented he made the speech of an honourable man, the speech of a true soldier, and even in his defence he revealed no departmental secrets. In that he was unlike the Minister of Militia who tells us whatever he pleases about Lord Dun-donald's report and then refuses to produce it. In a manly and straightforward way I.ord Dundonald answered the charges that had been made against him in public and in private.
Beyond that he ventured not a foot. I cannot understand how people, even to advance political interests, could pretend that in that speech and in that gathering there was anything political. Ask the people who were at it, unless paid partisans or representatives of party papers. It was a great spontaneous tribute which any man should be proud of. Now, with regard to the recall. Hon. gentlemen opposite shouted when they heard of it; but how has he been recalled ? We do not know. But I will venture to prophesy-because there is only one way, under British rule and British law, in which he can be recalled. He is no official of the British government. He was an official of Canada. When he was dismissed, he was free to discuss anything. I doubt if there is one hon. gentleman sitting on these treasury benches who would have kept his mouth closed as the general has done, about things which have happened in the department. He did not say anything about his report, but he did deny some which seemed inspired* from their knowledge of things unpublished as to the alleged ' Private ' report suppressed by the Minister of Militia. He acted as a gentleman, as he is ; he acted the man, who is more than the gentleman in some ways ; he acted not only the man but the brave man and the patriotic man ; he told the truth, and the people of this country will believe him. I want to tell these hon. gentlemen that in attempting to exploit this matter upon us, they are exploiting it upon themselves. They are suffering the consequences to-day, because the people will believe the man, not the politician, but the great imperial soldier that he is, and he tells the truth. As to his return, what is he to-day ? He is a soldier on half pay ; and you will find, with all this talk, that he is going home because he has been called home for some service. I want to say

and this is only incidental-that I never saw the general but twice, both times at dinners. He would not know me if he saw me on the street to-day. I know his aide-de-camp, whom I have met two or three times socially. I asked him when the general was going to leave, saying that I would like to call on him before he left; and he told me that he was going to leave the first of the week after next. I have got tired of all this talk about Lord Dundonald's recall. speechtext:
The matter which we were discussing when the House rose at one o'clock-the Dundonald incident, as it is usually called-has attracted, and is like-iy to attract, a good deal of attention in this country. I do not know that I should have thought it necessary to say anything at all on the subject on this occasion were it not for the very definite and explicit manner in which the hon. the Minister of Finance strove to fasten on the Liberal-Conservative party the charge of making this an issue in this country or, as he put it, exploiting this incident for political advantage. That charge has been made by a gentleman with a good deal of authority, and therefore is worth noticing, but that gentleman has not thought it necessary to support his assertion with any evidence whatever ; and I think it will not be difficult to show that. all the evidence tends to prove that while some effort has been made to turn this incident to political advantage, that effort has been entirely made by the Liberal party, led by no less a gentleman than the right hon. the First Minister. From the moment this incident became public, the government recognized how dangerous it was for them. They should have remembered, however, that the incident was not the creation of th'eir opponents or of Lord Dundonald, but

that it awes its existence to one of their own number, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). And it was not hard to see. from the moment this matter came before this House, that the government had made up their mind exactly what line they were going to take. The right hon. gentleman himself, on the first occasion, unquestionably decided that he would treat Lord Dun-donald as an opponent of his administration and an ally of the Conservative party, and practically accused him of endeavouring to dragoon the government of the day. And in order to make that charge as offensive as possible, he proceeded further to inform the House and the country that the one who was endeavouring to dragoon the government was a foreigner. Nothing could have been better devised to raise the 'feeling of the Liberal party against Lord Dundonald and any gentleman whom it might be the policy of the government to associate \yith him at a later stage of the affair. There could be no question at all from the very outset that the government had determined to stand bv the Minister of Agriculture and dismiss the General Officer Commanding ; and in order to justify their doing this, they determined to make it a political matter and fasten all the odium on the opposition. On general principles, we might at once conclude, from the fact that the Finance Minister accused the Conservative party of making capital out of this matter, that they themselves were doing the very thing with which they were charging their opponents. From the moment this incident became known to the people, the government treated Lord Dundonald with very little courtesy. He was spoken of by the First Minister as a stranger and a foreigner who had undertaken to dragoon the administration, and the Minister of Militia, a little later on, sneered at the general as a nobleman and a patrician, and said it was wonderful condescension on his part to speak to him. a plebeian and an ordinary citizen of Canada. It seems to me that it was anything but good taste for a gentleman known as Sir Frederick Borden to sneer at titles. If the Minister of Militia has a right to feel a reasonable pride in the fact that the British government has seen fit to honour him with the title of ' Sir,' he should have some respect for the higher title worn by Earl Dundonald. But the hon. gentleman was not the only one to indulge in that course. He was followed by my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Russell), who said, in a mocking tone : Is this a time for discoursing when we have to deal with lords and dukes ?

Will it be said that he is exploiting this incident for Conservative purposes ? Would it not rather be said that he is exploiting it for Liberal purposes ? And my hon. friend from Nova Scotia (Mr. Fielding) gets up and is so zealous in support of British connection and has such strong condemnation to utter of any one who would exploit such an incident for political purposes. Why, he never thought of such a thing and he is burdened with grief to think that any party would do it. Well, Mr. Speaker, I know that hon. gentleman, and I know his record, and the record of those who have been associated with him. And I know that in every case where we have had an opportunity of looking upon their deeds we have found that every act they condemn, they only wanted an opportunity to proceed to do in the most extreme manner themselves : if they denounced opponents for having taken any course, they only waited a chance to so completely outdo their opponents in that course that thereafter those opponents would never be mentioned in that connection. The people of this country know their record, that record of broken promises, absolute failure ever to do anything they promised, and of readiness to do everything that they had sworn not to do. So, there is no occasion to fear that the utterances of the Prime Minister or the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) will for a moment deceive the people of this country as to their course on this question. The Finance Minister has said that the government of this country is able to take care of itself. Unquestionably it is. He says that it has not appealed to the British government for any assistance. I presume not, since he says so. But I say this-that if the British government have recalled Dun-donald, then, it is perfectly true, as my hon. friend from South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) said that they could only recall him as a half-pay officer. They might invite him to return, but they could not order him to do so, except as half-pay officer. And, if they have recalled him it is probably because they desire to advance him to a position of higher honour and power. They know that his action was taken with a view to strengthen the defences of this country and so make Mr. BELL.
Canada more valuable as a part of the empire and to strengthen the bonds that unite it with the empire. The British government, if it has acted as suggested has acted very generously to the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his supporters. It is always inclined to do so. I presume it may have thought it expedient to do so. Because the threats-for Sir Elzear Taschereau did not hesitate to threaten the British government with the displeasure of this government, for he says, ' I cannot see how the British government, even in its own interest, can fail to recall Lord Dun-donald before the end of the week.' What interest of the British government was threatened by the presence of Lord Dun: donald in this country that Sir Elzear Taschereau must inform them that there was danger to that interest in allowing Lord Dundonald to remain here ? It strikes me th.\t this interview which purports to have been given by the Chief Justice is a forgery, or else Sir Elzear Taschereau was so ill-advised as to utter, in the course of his interview a threat-I was about to say a veiled threat, but it was not at all veiled, but very distinct and very plain, that the presence of Lord Dundonald in this country would militate against the interest of the empire and would justify this government in taking such a course as would not be in the interest of the British government. What else can the language mean, if it means anything at all ? But I do not believe for a moment that the British government in this case has done more or less than they have uniformly done in dealing with the government of the right hon. gentleman. They have acted with him and with the people of Canada as they have acted with all the colonies, in a most generous fashion. They are probably far enough away from this little matter to view it calmly, and probably to view it in its proper proportion. For, to my mind, it was not a great matter in the first instance, and, if the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) had acted with proper dignity and not descended to an attack on Lord Dundonald and every one who called himself Lord Dundon-ald's friend, it would never have been other than a small incident. But, as I say, the British government have acted generously ; they have acted as they do toward friend and foe, toward the colonies, toward the United States and toward every country with which they have any dealings, with the greatest magnanimity. If Lord Dun-donald's presence is embarassing to the administration, no doubt the British government is willing to withdraw him and, as far as possible, to relieve them from the embarrassment from which they are suffering. It is not the first time the British government have acted generously with hon. gentlemen opposite. For twenty years the Conservative party in this country, which certainly deserved well of the British govern-

ment if any party ever did, for there was never any question as to their willingness to do everything in their power to strengthen British connection and to make Canada a source of strength to the empire-for twenty years that party endeavoured in vain to have the Belgian and German treaties denounced by the government. And it was only when the present government had involved themselves in a morass of difficulties, after they had got into a slough of despond from which they could never hope to extricate themselves, that, to release them from their difficulties, the British government denounced those treaties. And, in this, case, also, if the British government have acted as stated, they have simply followed the course that they have always followed in acting generously to the hon. gentlemen opposite. And I think hon. gentlemen on this side have no objection to seeing that step taken by the British government. But we must remember that, in what they have done they have stretched their courtesy. Why should they have recalled Lord Dundonald from this country ? For, even if it can be proven that he was taking an active part in hostility to this government, is that a reason why the British government should take such a course ?
Why should they do it ? He was nj lo lger a servant of this government, but a halfpay officer of the British government. Major General Laurie was a half-pay officer of the imp.ri.il government when he carried the county of Shelburne and sat in this House as an active opponent of hon. gentlemen opposite. The Liberal-Conservative party are charged with taking such steps in this matter as would give a political eomplexiou to this Dundonald incident. They have never done so in any one respect. The courtesies shown to Lord Dundonald everywhere throughout Canada have been extended to him as a man and a soldier. column exploiting once more, for political purposes, the inadvertent use of the word ' foreigner ' by the Prime Minister. Mr. Speaker, I fancy it never has been challenged since the days when sundry gentlemen, at the time feeling somewhat sore over the Rebellion Losses Act, actually went so far as to rotton-egg the representative of His Majesty, Lord Elgin.
It is quite possible that it was impugned at a later date when the then leader of the Conservative party went so far as to say, in discussing a certain tariff issue, that if the result of the tariff then adopted, the national policy, was to injure British connection-then so much the worse for British connection. However, I would not willingly recall these matters had not the hon. gentleman practically challenged the loyalty of the great Liberal party of this country. For my part, I do not believe that there is isuch a thing as disloyalty in the Dominion of Canada. I have yet to meet a man, either Liberal or Conservative, who is disloyal. I believe we are true to the last man to Canada under British connection, but I do think it is bad taste indeed for hon. gentlemen opposite to rise in their places in the House and try to create the impression in Canada, yes, and beyond its borders, that the Liberal party, representing as it does more than half the people of Canada,

is absolutely disloyal to Canada and disloyal to the British empire.
But, enough of this. Let me rather come down to something which has arisen out of the recent utterances of Lord Dun-donald in regard to the administration of militia matters in Canada. I would refer to his phrases ' fool's paradise ' and ' government indifference to the militia.' I would call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that in the last three years we have spent $10,000,000 upon the militia of Canada, that this year we are spending $3,500,000 upon it and that we have increased the annual expenditure upon the militia by from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000. I do not believe you can find a greater test of the good wishes of the government towards any particular branch of the public service than that which is afforded by the estimates. If you find that the government is supporting a certain branch of the public service by liberal expenditures and taking the chance of criticism from the opposition and from those people in the country who are against large expenditures you may say at once that the government is not indifferent to that particular branch of the public service. But, if we live in a fool's paradise to-day what kind of a fool's paradise did we live in before 1896 ? The rules of the House will not permit me to characterize the kind of fool's paradise that we lived in prior to 1896. But then I can prove to you by comparison that it was certainly a very superlative kind of fool's paradise as compared with the fool's paradise in which we are said to exist now. We find that the government is now giving the militia of Canada annual drills. I have been in the militia of Canada for nine years under the late government and for eight years under this government, so that I think I am in a position to speak with some little knowledge and authority on this subject and I say that there never was anything more detrimental to the true interests of the militia than the system which was pursued under the Conservative government in this connection ; that is the system of calling out the militia every other year to get its training. I had almost made a bull by speaking of calling it out every other year to get its annual drill. As a matter of fact the regiments simply went to pieces because of inactivity, consequent upon the two years of idleness which intervened between one camp and another. It was reserved for this government under the energetic and able management of the present hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) to call the militia out every year, but two, I think, in full strength, and in these two years in very tolerable strength, the officers and noncommissioned officers and a portion of the rank and file being drilled during these two years. That fact is one of the best evidences that can be adduced in *proof of the interest that is being taken In the militia of Canada. Then, I am going to refer to something which, although it is a small matter, still has its significance. It was reserved to this government to obtain for the Fenian raid veterans medals which they had earned a third of a century ago. It was reserved for this government to obtain a long service medal for every officer and man who has served twenty years in the militia. It was reserved for this government to put an end to the life and good behaviour tenure of commanding officers, something utterly subversive of the best interests of the militia, because we found in regiment after regiment colonels who had retained their commands for periods ranging from twenty to thirty-five years, with the result that there was no promotion in the ranks junior to that of the commanding officer to be looked forward to and it was impossible to get men to go in and take an interest in such a force as that. If the government and if the active head of the Militia Department had been indifferent to the militia, do you imagine that these matters, some of them small in themselves, but which are somewhat important to the militia, would have received their close attention, the best evidence of which is that these changes have been made ? Not at all. But, let me give a little further testimony. What about the cadet corps to-day ? It was reserved for this government to develop this system of cadet corps. To-day, we have thousands of boys coming up in the schools all over the country getting their preliminary drill and their training in the art of rifle shooting in consequence of the energy and thoughtfulness of this government and entirely in the absence of any thing being done under the old government. We have organized an army medical corps. We have a splendid army medical staff and bearer corps. Whereas in the past hon. gentlemen opposite had their regimental surgeon with his little pill-box. we have this army medical corps with field hospitals and stretchers for the wounded men and officers of the militia force, all of which are necessary to an army in the field. If an army corps were called upon to-day to go upon active service it would take no time to organize the medical part of the army corps because we have the nucleus for doing it and inasmuch as that ife a scientific branch of the service it is something that could not be improved or dealt with in a haphazard way. But, as a result of the organization of this service our fellows, if they were called upon to take the field, would have careful treatment for their wounds or in case of disease.

'Mr. WARD. Under -what General Officer Commanding were these improvements made ?

speechtext:
These improvements were made under the present government ; I do not care from what General Officer commanding the suggesting came. As I understand it, it is the government that has the power of the purse-strings and the power to say whether this or that shall or shall not be done, and the members of the government, as wise men will take the advice of experts. We do not necessarily expect those in the civil departments to be experts in certain lines themselves, but if they take expert testimony, and if having obtained good advice, they act upon it, then they deserve the credit if they give us a good up to date system. We have an intelligence department which we were before entirely without. This department is made up of picked men, selected from the militia in various parts of Canada to collect information which would be of the greatest practical use in case the force was called out upon active service. We have organized the engineers, another corps, that cannot be improvised. We may have had a few in the, old days, very few, but today we have an engineer corps which is a most useful part of the militia force and in the city of Toronto that corps has been organized in connection with the school of practical science which increases its usefulness, because as young men finish their course in the school of science they scatter through Canada and each man becomes a valuable instructor in each particular locality. The government have organized rifle clubs and established rifle ranges. These are things upon which we all agree in this House. Everybody says that our young men in Canada ought to be taught how to shoot. My hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) said within the last week that he heartily approved of this plan and that he would use his best endeavours to encourage the practice of rifle shooting in the part of the country from which he came.
