That was unworthy of any man outside of this House, and much more unworthy of any one who has the honour of a seat here. If such a statement is made here, it should be made upon proof, instead of being put in the form of an insinuation against a man who is not here to defend himself, and to whom, if they could, these hon. gentlemen would deny even the right to speak on his own behalf on the public platform.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, not to attack Lord Dundonald, nor to defend him, but merely to draw attention to two striking omissions in the observations of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). When the motion was made this morning that you leave the chair, the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) called attention to two utterances of a member of this government who is now in the old country, one touching the Dundonald incident and the other on the subject of preferential trade. Regarding the Dundonald incident, the right hon. gentleman who leads the House (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) very properly took the ground that it was not fair to attack a public man on the ground of reported utterances of his unless it was shown that those utterances had been revised by himself. If so I can quite see that it would be improper to condemn the Solicitor General until his words had been proved to be those with which he was charged. But, Sir, even while the right hon. gentleman so spoke, it seems to me that a glorious opportunity was afforded him. Without in any way repudiating his Solicitor General he could have said, disbelieving that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) spoke as he was charged, that had his Solicitor General so spoken, had he said that unless Lord Dundonald was recalled within a week it would be an attack upon the Laurier government, he (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) might have repudiated any such statement as that. The right hon. gentleman in addressing that House on that utterance of the Solicitor General, in no way repudiated the sentiment alleged to have been uttered by that gentleman, and when he went on to attack Lord Dundonald for his conduct, the one conclusion that could be come to by the House and the country was that when the right hon. gentleman abstained from expressing any difference in opinion from the alleged utterance of the Solicitor General that he agreed with the Solicitor General in- the utterance he had made. It seemed to me that all throughout this discussion not only today but on other occasions the main point at issue has not always been reached by hon. gentlemen on either side. It always seems to me that there is a great desire on Mr. SPROULE.
the part of the government and its supporters to concentrate attention on the fact that Lord Dundonald was guilty of an indiscreet utterance and was punished therefor. If Lord Dundonald was guilty of an indiscreet utterance and was punished therefor that question is closed and we have nothing more to do with it. But I venture to say that the members of this House and the people of this country are deeply interested in the charges made by Lord Dundonald and the point which this country would like to see cleared up is whether the charges of Lord Dundonald are true or false. If they are true, a lamentable state of affairs exists in our militia system. If they are false, the sooner, for their own sake, the government prove them false the better. To show how hard it is for ordinary laymen like myself to discover the truth in regard to the militia system let me remind the House of the utterances of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. A. T. Thompson) this afternoon. That gentleman is always eloquent, and always speaks well and I will do him the justice of saying that I never knew him more eloquent and apparently sincere than he was this afternoon. When I heard his glowing eulogium on the militia system and the credit which he gave to the government, and especially to the Militia Department, on the industry, ability and skill which had been brought to bear on the militia forces in the last eight years, when in tones of proud triumph he called attention to the fact that in the last three years-that is not including this year-we had actually spent $10,000,000 for the improvement of the militia system, I was reminded of an incident which occurred in this House only a short year ago. In my effort to discover the real situation as to the Militia Department I referred back to the ' Hansard ' and now let me give the House the opinion of an expert, a colonel commanding a regiment, speaking in this House with a full sense of responsibility. This is what the House was then told :
Well, Sir, in all seriousness, after due consideration and recognizing the importance of the assertion, I say here to-day in my place in parliament that the militia, so far as the rural part thereof is concerned is in an infinitely worse plight to-day than it was two years ago, and that in my opinion another year under present 'conditions will utterly demoralize it.
That, Sir, is the opinion of an expert, the colonel of a battalion only one short year ago. Let me go further. I find in the same speech, this sentence :
I have shown that we were called upon to furnish the skeleton of a skeleton, I now state that we have actually turned out the shadow of a skeleton of a skeleton. Can anything so ghost-like be longer called a militia force. True the officers and non-commissioned officers, the most important part, showed up in very fair numbers, but this will not continue. Men must have a pride in their unit

or they will cease to act. I know the case oi one company which this year had two officers and six non-commissioned officers to command two men, one of whom was the cook.
Perhaps the Minister of Militia can inform us how many of these officers now belong to the corps in which seven lieutenant-colonels are required to command 100 men. This apparently is above that average, two officers and six non-commissioned officers to command two men, one of whom was the cook. And that was the Canadian militia system under the admirable administration of hon. gentlemen opposite at the end of three years, during which we spent $10,000,000 to secure their efficiency. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. A. T. Thompson) this afternoon said that the only fault he had to find with the government last year was the meagreness of the pay. This gentleman last year, addressing the House, said :
A great deal of unnecessary trouble was caused this year by withholding notice for camp until within from three weeks to ten days of the time ordered. Knowing that some regiments were not to be called out, a feeling of uncertainty pervaded the whole, and I can assure you that recruiting is too unpleasant a job to be undertaken on chances. When the summons did come, it was found that some of the best regiments had been overlooked.
That, Sir, is an opinion of the administration of the militia by the Militia Department given by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. A. T. Thompson) in this House last year. I do not wish to contradict anything he said to-day. Far be it from me to impute any improper motives to him, but surely we are entitled to some explanation from the hon. gentleman which will account for the marvellous discrepancy between the statement made a year ago and the statement given to this House to-day. That hon. gentleman gloried in the fact that in the last three years we had spent $10,000,000 on militia affairs, and were spending this present year $3,000,000. Does he not see that that proves the loyalty and generosity of this House, and it proves the confidence the representatives of the people had that the people would support any reasonable expenditure to maintain the efficiency of our militia. But, Sir, what sort of a commentary is it that $10,000,000 have been spent on the militia and at the end of three years that is all we have to show V Surely it is not in the interests of this country that we should have an hon. minister at the head of the department quarrelling with and dismissing a gentleman who is admitted to be the most competent man we ever had in such a position in Canada, a gentleman who, during the last year by the assurance of the hon. member for Haldimand this afternoon, has raised the militia to a degree of efficiency that could not have been conceived possible a year 227i
ago. What are we to think of the business ability of the head of a department who will lose the services of such a man for such a paltry incident, take it at the very worst, as that he spoke inadvisedly at an inopportune time ? Surely the interest of the people of this country should be considered. It is all very well for the ministers to be touchy about their own dignity and importance, but in view of the statement made by the hon. member for Haldimand a year ago and to-day, the people of this country have some right to ask where we are when this business administration deprives us of the services of the best man we ever had, shutting the door for ever to the coming to Canada of such another man, for having made the statement that a minister had interfered outside his own department, in the Militia Department, a statement which that minister himself has admitted during this session was true to the very letter. So we have this conceded that Lord Dundonald has spoken the truth from beginning to end and Lord Dundonald is punished, the Canadian militia must lose his services, simply because he told the truth. There is of course an old saying that the greater the truth, sometimes the greater the libel.
I wish to protest against the attention of this House being called exclusively to the question whether or not Lord Dundonald was right or whether or not Lord Dundonald should have been dismissed when the real question that now interests us, the incident of the dismissal having been closed, is what we are getting for the $10,000,000 we have spent and the $3,000,000 we are spending this year.
There is one other question raised by the quotation from the speech of the Solicitor General read by the leader of the opposition, and I was surprised at the Finance Minister not referring to it. The Solicitor General, speaking in the old country, must of necessity speak with a certain authority. I do not propose this afternoon to blame him for what he said. If I were to blame him for what he said, I would be blaming myself, inasmuch as a short time ago, I said that I thought it was only reasonable that a man should not be judged by newspaper reports). Therefore, I do not intend to blame the hon. Solicitor General so much for what he did say, but I desire to call the attention of the House to the opportunity that presented itself to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) when he rose to speak, it being particularly within his functions, in regard to the alleged statement of the lion. Solicitor General that Canada did not want a preference for what we had given to the old country by way of the preferential tariff because we had given it freely and ungrudgingly without desiring anything in return. This is perhaps the most important question that is now before any portion of

the British empire to-day. We must remember that we have a fiscal warfare going on in the old country at the present time. Great Britain is distracted as it has not been since the days of the Reform Bill or possibly the Repeal of the Corn Laws over this great question of preferential trade. We know that it has been said in the old country by some that representatives of the present government, when attending the conference there a few years ago, expressed their approval of the principle of preferential trade. We know that in the election of 1890, when the right hon. Prime Minister went to London, Out., he delivered a speech on the subject of preferential trade, when, to do the right hon. gentleman justice, I think he made the ablest and most eloquent presentation of the advantages of preferential trade to Canada that I have ever seen or heard, a presentation that must have convinced every one present, of the benefit and advantages that would accrue to Canada. He went on in his powerful appeal to point out from his standpoint that he and his party were the only ones who could secure this great boon for Canada, that the Conservative party could not secure this boon saying : Place me and my party in power and our first duty will be to secure preferential trade. No more powerful argument could be addressed to the people than that which was used by the right hon. Prime Minister. So, there are some people in the old country, who, knowing what took place in the Intercolonial Conference, and knowing of such utterances as that by the right hon. Prime Minister, believe that this government is in favour of preferential trade. There are others in the old country who, being deceived by the position which the right hon. gentleman took at the Cobden club, are convinced that this government is opposed to preferential trade. What a glorious opportunity was given this morning to the hon. Minister .of Finance or to the right hon. Prime Minister, without agreeing with or disagreeing from the utterances of the Solicitor General to say : If he did use that language we repudiate it because we are in favour of preferential trade. If the government desire preferential trade the government could have done more in one minute this morning by such an utterance as that from the hon. Minister of Finance than the opposition could do by six months of touring through the country and speaking from every platform from the Atlantic to the Pacific.' I appeal to the government and I ask them to take advantage of this chance. One of the reasons why I rose this afternoon was to call the right hon. Prime Minister's attention to the fact that the government are already committed to the principle of preferential trade and here to-day, without a vote of the House, with one single utterance, he to-day, could have given an impetus to the cause of preferential trade, if it would be the boon to Canada which the Mr. NORTHRUP.
right hon. Prime Minister proved it would be, and in that I heartily agree with him. If he had done so he would have done more for Canada than he has done in many a day gone by. But, I can see that the hon. Minister of Finance was embarrassed because the hon. Solicitor General, speaking with a certain amount of authority, is reported to have said that we were not in favour of a preference because we have given a preference to the mother country without expecting anything in return. The right hon. Prime Minister, I remember, when speaking two years ago, flatly contradicted that utterance. We have his statement on 'Hansard' that we did not give this preference as a matter of gratitude expecting no return, but that there were sound business reasons for giving this preference, that it was a benefit to ourselves, that it would get us goods cheaper-good sound free trade doctrine-and that it was hoped that as a result of giving them this preference they would give us something in return. There seems to-day to be a large portion of people in the mother country who are ready to give us something in return and I would appeal to the hon. minister to take advantage of such an opportunity and state frankly that the preference was given in the hope that we would be given something in return. And that we are prepared to deal with the mother country along this line. I would endorse the hon. minister in going further, having said that much, and saying that if the mother country declines to deal with us in the matter of a preference we will have to recall what we have done, having done it in good faith and having failed. I sincerely hope that the charge that has been made by the government against the opposition and the like charge which has been made in the old country will turn out to be without ground ; that is that the opposition are trying to exploit Lord Dundonald for their own purposes. I have no hesitation in saying that if the opposition were to take hold of the Dundonald incident and endeavour to use Lord Dun-donald's sympathy for party purposes they would be unworthy of their positions in this House, but, I can quite understand altogether apart from party ideas, that, be they Reformers or Conservatives, Scotch, Irish or English, the citizens of Canada who have an admiration for Lord Dundonald regret the particular mode in which he is leaving the country. I can quite understand that they feel it due to this gentleman who came to Canada, who has done so much for the militia as the hon. gentleman foT Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) has proved this afternoon, and who has to leave this country under circumstances which are very much to be deplored, should desire to show to him and show to the world, that, whether he was right or wrong in that particular, small controversial question, Canada believes he was true to Canada and true to the empire.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I miglit not be excused for taking part in this debate if it were strictly a military or militia matter, not being a military or militia man, but as it appears to be largely a political matter I presume I have the privilege of addressing the House. The question, as far as I understand, which has been particularly argued to-day is as to whether Lord Dundonald has or has not been exploited as a political issue by the opposition party. Apparently that question has aroused the interest of a more important body than ourselves, apparently the decision there has been that he has been made a political issue by the party of the opposition, and apparently that decision has not found favour op the other side of the House. To-day we have had the tune carried from treason by the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to blasphemy by the hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) in expressing their views in regard to this matter. For my own part I think we might consider it in a little different light from that in which it has been considered so far in the debate. As to whether hon. gentlemen opposite are exploiting Lord Dundonald as a political issue or not-I think they have afforded the proof to-day. They have denied and reiterated the denial with a persistence that I think would entitle them to the appellation given by Lord Beaconsfield to his opposition at one time ; that is to say, an organized hypocrisy, for if any body of men have without regard to rhyme or reason taken Lord Dundonald as a political issue it is our friends of the opposition and their party press. I will not depend upon mere assertion to prove this. I suppose every one will admit that the Montreal ' Gazette ' is an exponent of the Conservative party, and its leading exponent if the test of respectability is to be applied. In the Montreal ' Gazette ' of July 16, I find the following paragraph in the editorial notes :
Goldwin Smith thinks a great wrong is^ being done Lord Dundonald by making his difficulties with the government a party question. There is no necessity for worrying. It will not be a party question after the Laurier government has been buried under in the next election.
If that is not a plain and explicit statement by the leading and most respectable organ of the Conservative party, that with Lord Dundonald they expect to win the coming elections, I admit that I do not understand the English language. I will not burden ' Hansard ' with other quotations of similar character, but every gentleman of this House can read such expressions in the Conservative newspapers from day to day and from week to week. I cannot imagine what is the purpose of hon. gentlemen opposite in making the preposterous assertion in this House that they have not carried Lord Dundonald into their politics,
for surely they cannot expect that the country, much less their own constituents, will believe it.
But, Sir, there is something more than this exploiting of Lord Dundonald by the Conservative party. I have noticed that their campaign has lagged considerably of late, until to-day the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), revived the silly Slander against the Prime Minister in connection with bis use of the word ' foreigner ' as applied to Lord Dundonald. I may be par-donald for putting this case in a way in which I have not yet heard it put. It is within the knowledge of every member of this House, and within the knowledge of every man in the Dominion who read the remarks of the Prime Minister, that instead of making the most remote allusion to Lord Dundonald as a foreigner or a stranger to the Dominion of Canada, the expression was simply applied -to Lord Dundonald as a stranger in the eastern townships, a fact which no one will deny, and least of all Lord Dundonald himself. That being the case, the expression cannot ;be construed as being in any way offensive to Lord Dundonald or as properly or improperly describing his connection with Canada. When these gentlemen opposite carry on this campaign in such a way, and then come to the House and declare that there is no politics in it, it is an evidence of hypocrisy that has seldom been equalled in this little world of ours.
The conduct of the Conservative party in this campaign, reminds me that .when some nations which are neither honourable nor courageous are engaged in warfare, they, upon occasion, place their women, their children or their hostages between themselves and the enemy, and then should these be injured by the bullets of the enemy, they raise the cry that non-combatants are being-slaughtered. If Lord Dundonald is not a party to this political campaign, the Conservatives in this country are putting Lord Dundonald in front of their battle ranks and holding him there to receive the attacks that may be made on them. Then they complain that Lord Dundonald is attacked.
Well, Sir, we will not attack Lord Dundonald; we will get around behind Lord Dundonald and just for one moment discuss the position of these gentlemen who are using him in this dishonourable way. The charge made by Lord Dundonald against this government ; the charge that has a purpose and that means something to the people of Canada, is, that the government has neglected the militia corps. That charge is the gravest one that could be made_ against any Canadian government, because it means disloyalty to Canada and disloyalty to the empire if it be true. I say, Sir, that this government does not suffer by a comparison of their loyalty either to Canada or to the empire, with the loyalty of the govern-

meats which have preceded them and which are honoured by the support of the Conservative party. Who speaks of loyalty to the empire ? The empire has been engaged in many wars during the last half century, but it was a Liberal government that first sent Canadian soldiers to take part in the wars of the empire. It was a Liberal government who did this, and Sir, it was the very government whose loyalty forsooth is called in question by members of the opposition, and by insinuations made against it by Lord Dundonald. When has occasion arisen for the manifestation of loyalty to the empire, that the Liberal government of Canada has not responded V In case of war the instance is recent, in matters of trade the instance is almost as recent. It was a chieftain of the Conservative party who once said : If our tariff is bad for British connection, so much the worse for British connection. And, yet, the followers of that chieftain are the men who to-day charge disloyalty against this government which has given the British rna'uu-facturer a preference in Canada and asked for no return. But more than that, because it did not ask for a return in kind from the motherland, this government is accused by the Conservative party of disloyalty to Canada and to Canadian interests, and in every manufacturing city in the Dominion the campaign is daily waged against it on that ground. We do not fear a comparison of our loyalty with the loyalty of the Conservative party. Whether in French Canada or in English Canada, the Liberal party has been true and loyal to the British empire.
And now a few words in regard to Lord Dundonald himself. Lord Dundonald is spoken of as a soldier and a gentleman ; a great soldier and a noble gentleman. We do not find fault with either his military title or his civil standing. He is welcome to it all, and our friends on the other side are welcome to all the advantage the qualities of Lord Dundonald bring them, when they use him for their party purposes. But,
I would like to call the attention of the House and of the country to this fact: That Lord Dundonald cannot be protected in the mantle of his noble lineage and his high military position, and at the same time act as a party hack and agent of the Conservative party.	'

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
All right-and on the ground of his military position. It has been questioned to-day whether Lord Dundonald had a right to speak out as he has done on political platforms here and there throughout this country. No man properly questions his right. He had a perfect right to do so to go on the platform in Toronto and speak his mind, and make such charges as he pleased against the government of this country-to charge disloyalty if he liked ; but he cannot expect to be protected in doing so by the sanctity of his position ; and that is what hon. members seem to hope that he is able to do. They hope to get the advantage of a nobleman and a general of the British army fighting in their ranks, while he, so to speak, shall be encased in 'that divinity which doth hedge about a king,' and which shall prevent legitimate criticism by his and their opponents.
Let us judge the action of Lord Dundonald by the standards that would be applied to a common, every-day colonial civilian-the Minister of Agriculture if you like-and see just how he stands, and whether he is or is not a partisan of hon. gentlemen opposite. I was struck by a very strong expression which his lordship used in his speech in Toronto. He said he had turned the search-light on the inner workings of the Militia Department. I think a little turning of the search-light on the action of his lordship on that particular occasion would not be amiss. Under wlsat circumstances did he turn on the search-light, and what was the occasion ? The occasion was a private or semi-private banquet given in his honour by militia officers of the city and district of Montreal. The banquet, I say, was private or semiprivate, I am not prepared to say which ; but it was certainly not public, inasmuch as only one newspaper was represented at it-so the newspaper itself has stated. Lord Dundonald has told us in his manifesto and on the platform that he had great grievances against this government of Canada, that the empire had great grievances against 3.11, that the loyal people of this country hjad great grievances against it, because of its neglect of Canada's imperial de-fe nces ; that we were living in a fool's paradise at the mercy of our neighbours because of the neglect of this government. Could language be stronger ? Could charges be more severe ? Lord Dundonald did not deal with those charges at that Montreal banquet-a proper matter to be dealt with, if ever there was one, at a strictly military banquet. That surely would have been a subject worthy of turning the search-light on ; but it was not upon that subject that he turned the search-light. His search-light was turned upon the inner workings of the department.

It was turned upon the appointment of one Dr. Picltel to a position in the militia force ; and when the question came to be thrashed out in parliament-and: it has never yet been denied-the position of the Minister of Agriculture was found to be the correct position, and the position of Lord Dundonald the wrong position, looked at from a strictly military point of view. The Minister of Agriculture had asked that a competent man be placed in a position requiring competence. Lord Dundonald was offended because a man who was not competent was not placed in that position. The charge was not even made against the Militia Department of which he was an official and with which he was connected ; it was made against the government of the day through the Minister of Agriculture. The charge was political interference under the administration of the government of the day. It was not a military matter ; it was not a militia matter ; it was not turning the search-light on the defenceless condition of Canada. What was it ? If the Minister of Agriculture or some other plain colonial had attended a banquet as a guest under such circumstances, and had made that statement to the gentlemen present, what would he have been doing ? He would have been attempting to arouse political dissatisfaction and animosity in the minds of the officers of the militia there present against the government of the day. Lord Dundonald was not turning any search-light on, because it was a private or semi-private banquet, and not a public demonstration. It was so private that his remarks were not published when the proceedings of the banquet were published. They were suppressed- ' suppressed ' is the word used-at the request of Lord Dundonald's friends. Did he turn on. the search-light ?[DOT] It was only when some injudicious partisan of the opposition, having heard accidentally of the remarks of Lord Dundonald, thought they were too good to let drop. He wanted to use such good political ammunition in public. He was not willing to let it go as it was intended to go and stay where it was intended to stay, where it would poison the minds of the officers of the militia against the administration, but would not bring discredit upon the General Officer Commanding. But when this injudicious newspaper friend gave the matter to the light of day, and when his lordship was called in question about it by the militia authorities, when he was brought to the mark and had to either say that he had said it or take it back, then he turned the searchlight on. I take the liberty of saying that the action of Lord Dundonald at that banquet in Montreal, what he said and the way he said it, is fair evidence that what he did there he had been doing on
previous occasions, and had he not been brought to book at that time, he would have been doing it yet. And what would he have been doing ? Acting as the political agent of the party of the opposition, abusing his position as an officer of the imperial government and as an officer of the government of Canada, for the purpose of advancing the party interests of hon. gentlemen opposite. What else ? Had a private individual done this, no one would have had a word to say in his defence. How much more guilty then was Lord Dundonald, who lent the prestige of his name and reputation to everything he !said ? Let us have fair play in this matter. Let us deal with these things on a fair footing and call them by their right names. If we are to have fair play, let us have it ; and if we are to have treachery, let us have treachery and deal with it as such.
This incident does not stand alone. Some weeks have passed since that time, during which Lord Dundonald has been the recipient of numbers of demonstrations in his honour. It was the privilege of Canadian citizens to (give such demonstrations in his honour as they wished, and the privilege of Lord Dundonald to accept them 'if he saw fit to do so. He saw fit to accept them as being strictly non-political. They were given to and accepted by him as non-political. There was a demonstration in Renfrew and another in Ottawa in his honour, and it was perfectly understood of both of these that they were strictly non-political. A demonstration was offered him by the people of Toronto, which, it was also understood, would be strictly non-political as were the others. I presume that that demonstration was accepted by His Lordship on the same understanding ias were the others. There were many people gathered in Toronto at that meeting for the purpose of doing honour to His LordShip and the position he held in the army and the English nobility. No doubt many were present who felt aggrieved at his dismissal and others who acquiesced in that dismissal, as I believe every member of the opposition does, because although that question has been raised two or three times in the House, not one member of the opposition has ever dared to challenge a vote of the House on the course taken by the government or so place on record his views with regal'd to it. People went to that non-political demonstration, knowing it be such on the authority of the chairman of the committee. But what happened ? Lord Dundonald made there a violent attack on the government of this country. He abused as he had done before, the position in which he found himself. This we have on the authority of Mr. Ellis, the chairman of the committee. He took advantage of the idemonstration. in which he must have known there were Liberals taking part, to make a violent attack on the government

7147
and its policy. He had a perfect right to do so as a citizen, but he cannot be upheld in doing so as a man of strict honour. I think it is -well that we should have a straight understanding with regard to this question, and just in order that there may be no mistake in regard to what I say, let me quote the words of Mr. Ellis, as published in an interview which appeared in the Toronto ' World.' Mr. Ellis, I may say, is a leading Conservative of the city of Toronto. In that interview he said :
I was surprised at the whole tenor of his remarks. I do not think the committee expected it ; I certaiDly did not.
There was therefore a distinct breach of faith with the committee which organized this demonstration-at least as far as the chairman was concerned and a large number of those who attended. It appears that his attitude and the remarks he made were so far aside from what was expected, so far regardless of propriety, that they brought about this discussion in the British House of Commons, and the statement by the Secretary of War that he has been requested to return to England to speak in his own defence. I was somewhat amused at the construction placed upon this statement by the hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale). He said he would venture the prophecy that Lord Dundonald was being recalled in order to give him some higher position. Well, although I am not familiar with the workings of the British government. I know that it is customary in the management of public affairs in that country for the government, when they find it necessary to discipline some of its high officials, to let them down easy by ap-ponting them to some other office. We have heard of appointments to the Chiltern Hundreds, and there are other appointments of a like character. It is quite possible that Lord Dundonald may receive some such appointment from the British government, and no one here will object to anything which the British government may do with or for him. But I would like to call attention to this fact, and I think it is perfectly right that I should do so, because we have heard a great deal about the transcendent military ability of Lord Dundonald. If he is a great military genius, if he has a great military record, then certainly, let the cause be what it may, the loss of his services to Canada will be considerable. But if it should happen peradventure that his record is not so transcendent, that his abilities are not so marvellous, then the loss to Canada will be considerably minimized. And in looking over the papers, I find that at the time when the British army needed the best officers it could get, at a time of Stress and trouble, the British government apparently did not think sufficiently of those transcendent abilities or t'his marvellous record to appoint Lord Dundonald to a com-Mr. OLIVER.
mand in South Africa. He went there just as our friend from North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) did, as a soldier of fortune, and secured an appointment in the field after he got there.

Therefore, I am bound to suppose, in view of all the circumstances, that, when His Lordship comes to take his place in the fighting ranks of the members of the opposition as a soldier of fortune once more, neither will they gain so much, nor will Canada lose so much by being deprived of his military services. We do not grudge hon. gentlemen opposite their new recruit. We wish him luck of the company he has, and we wish them luck of the qualifications he has) brought ho them. maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
The last speaker (Mr. Oliver) has echoed, perhaps in stronger language than we have heard from other members, but probably all the more truly, the sentiments of the members of the government towards Lord Dundonald ; in fact, has expressed them with a frankness which they have not yet ventured. They

have made the charge that Lord. Dundonald is being exploited by the Conservatives for political purposes. I make the charge that Lord Dundonald was exploited, was intended to be exploited and is being exploited by the party of lion, gentlemen opposite, for political purposes entirely. I attended |the meeting in Toronto he'd in honour of Lord Dundonald. It was a spontaneous tribute to that gentleman, such a meeting as I never thought to see, such as I never thought could be held in any city or any community. It was not a political gathering ; it was an expression of feeling by the people themselves. No political party could ever expect to hold such a meeting. I want to answer one charge made by the last speaker-and it is the only one I shall deal with-that Lord Dundonald committed a breach of faith in making the statement he did. I lunched with Lord Dundonald on the day of the meeting. I only arrived in town that day, but found the invitation to lunch awaiting me. I sat next to the chairman, Mr. Ellis. I asked him what the proceedings at the meeting were to be. He told me who the speakers were. I asked him what Lord Dundonald had to say, and he told me that the committee had discussed that, and that they had decided that they would make absolutely no allusion to politics, but that Lord Dundonald was free to say what he liked ; they had never spoken to him, or suggested that his utterance should be restrained. I think that that answers the charge. That meeting, being such as 1 have described was, it seems to me, compensation to Lord Dundonald for all the discredit the present government hoped would be cast upon him. It was a meeting to compensate any man for misfortunes of that kind. Do you mean to tell me, Mr. Speaker, that five thousand people went to that hall expecting to hear Lord Dundonald speak about the weather, or to ask them how they did ? They expected to hear Lord Dundonald defend himself-not so much against the charges made in this House, because he had a reply to the charges made here, though the minister tried to suppress it-but to those base slanders issued against him by the various newspaper organs of this government. He was perfectly entitled to reply to these charges, to reply to them in the strongest manner possible ; and I will venture to say that of the 5,000 people who were in that hail 4,900 went away perfectly satisfied with what Lord Dundonald had said on that occasion. If this is made a party matter, if it is made more a party matter than is necessary, the fault is entirely with the government and the manner in which they have dealt with this question. What is a rarty matter, and. one that the opposition are .qujite right in taking up, is the report that Lord Dundonald had read in this House as to the condition of the militia. And one point every speaker on the other side has tried to
avoid-has tried to lead the discussion off to side issues by attempting to make this a personal issue between the government and Lord Dundonald-and that point, the main point which the people want to know, and do know by the utterances of the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) is that the government are interfering for po'i-tical reasons with the militia of this country. Take that fact away, and the whole matter would fall as flat as any agitation ever did. That is the one point in which the people are primarily interested. On that point they believe Lord Dundonald absolutely, and he tells them that the militia is being made a political engine. We had the denial of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) on that point when the matter was first brought up ; we had his unqualified acceptance of it and his admission that this was the truth, before he sat down. We had the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Bcrden) also accepting it, though it was strongly denied at first. And when bon. members opposite got used to it, one after another verified (the (statement that the militia was as much a party question as the letting of contracts or the appointments to be made from one end of this country to the other. That is the point that interested the people-not the personality of Lord Dundonald-not the fact of his dismissal- but the fact that he has turned the searchlight on the scheme of this government to make a political engine of the m'li ia of this country. Now, the dismissal of Lord Dundonald, as one hon. gentleman said, would have passed off with very little comment had it not been that the manner of that dismissal roused the feelings of the people. I venture to say that there is not a business man in this House on either side who would have dismissed the lowest clerk in his employ, even for the gravest offense, unless it were an offence against honesty, as Lord Dundonald was dismissed by this government. To an outsider it would look as if they delibsrately considered how they could heap the greatest insult upon him. And, to my mind, that is the gravest charge next to the charge that has been proved and accepted-that the ministers are debasing the militia of this country into a mere political machine, which, as I say, is the point that is most regarded and most keenly resented by the people. Now, quotations have been made from the London despatches. Those against the government, the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), tells us, must not be accepted because they may not , be true. But those in favour of the government bon. gentlemen opposite accept without hesitation. Yet the very despatches that they object to are those that are sent over by the Canadian Associated Press which are paid for by this government to the amount of $15,000 a year. Now, let me read the closing word s of one of the speeches, that of Mr. Lloyd George, Liberal. He says :

It was grossly unfair and mischievous i/hat Lord Dundonald should he allowed to stir up strife-a feud between the two races in Canada.
Now. Sir, Lord Dundonald in his speech in Toronto made a very pleasing and earnest reference to the" French Canadians of Canada. He stated that in all his military career and since he came here he had made no distinctions between religions and nationalities and he also stated that he had the greatest admiration for the French Canadian citizens. He spoke with enthusiasm, and no part of his speech was received with greater enthusiasm by that vast audience than the sentiment expressed from his heart on that one point. No man could have spoken more earnestly, no remarks could have been more appreciated. Now let me read an extract from a telegram to the Toronto ' Globe,' of December 20, 1901. It is as follows :
London, Dec. 12.
The meeting at Birmingham has sent the following telegram to Mr. Chamberlain :- Lloyd George, the traitor, was not allowed to say a word. The citizens have passed resolutions, expressing confidence in the government, and their admiration of your unique and fearless services for King and country.
That is the class of men who are making mischief in this country. Can you imagine a man who is doing more mischief than such a one as this, who makes false statements, who puts false views into the mouth of any man in this country, publishes them in England, whence the Canadian Associated Press, paid for by this government, cables them out here That is the kind of literature that makes trouble, if trouble there is, between the nationalities. I listened with pleasure to the remarks of the hon. member for South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) and I think that if we all paid attention and took to heart the words which he spoke we would be the better for it. I can assure any one of my French Canadian fellow citizens, on that side of the House or on this side, that if they come to Toronto or to any other place in Ontario they will have a reception as cordial, as enthusiastic as they will get anywhere in their own province.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: From the Conservatives.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I will not say from the Conservatives, but from the Orangemen. I am not a member of that body. From the people of Ontario the French Canadians will get the warmest possible reception. I deplore greatly that there should be this constant bandying of words as to differences between one nationality and another. If it should be so that there was a feeling of hostility it should be the duty of every one of us to try and overcome that because we have to live together in this country, whether we like it or not. There is no such feeling, Mr. Speaker, in Ontario, and I Mr. OSLER.
say that it is despatches of this sort, the work of these mischief makers, who are looking through every page of the newspapers to clip a word here and there, publish them, and magnify them, that are making the mischief and trouble and I appeal to every member of this House to, as far as he can, endeavour to put a stop to that state of affairs.
At the meeting in Toronto, Lord Dundonald said :
I bad almost forgotten to mention one other charge insinuated against me in parliament, of having made a difference between a French Canadian officer and an Englishspeaking one-in favour of the latter. I have already shown in the paper and it has not been contradicted, how groundless was this charge. Here in this great capital of the great English-speaking province of Ontario I desire to say that no man's race or religion has ever biased me. The French Canadian militia know full well that I have always had their interests at heart and have been actuated by the utmost possible friendliness for them.
That statement was cheered to the echo, and I know that sentiment is the sentiment of the people of Ontario, notwithstanding the trouble that men like Lloyd George tried to bring about. Let me repeat that the charge that the Conservative party are endeavouring to make political capital out of this Dundonald matter is absolutely untrue. If political capital is to be made out of it the charge is to be laid at the door of the members of the government and their supporters who have from the very beginning of this question endeavoured to abuse Lord Dundonald, to make it a personal matter as against Lord Dundonald, to connect him with the opposition, so that they may hide away from the public gaze the grave charge which His Lordship has made that the government are debasing the militia for party purposes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: They are doing this, as my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) says, on Lord Dundonald's recommendation. It was rather amusing to listen to the speeches of the hon. member for Alberta and the hon. member for Haldimand. They both set up a straw man. and, as it were in strident tones, knocked him down again. I have never heard any charge of disloyalty made against the Liberal party from this side of the House, and yet these hon. gentlemen spent several minutes in trying to prove that such a charge had been made ; and after setting up this straw man, they undertook to knock him down again. We all believe in our loyalty, and there is not a man on this side of the House or on the other side who is required to say anything about it. The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, I am glad to say, is not in his place, but

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I am here.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I see the hon. gentleman. The hon. member for Alberta said, in the course of his remarks, that Lord Dundonald was altogether wrong all through these proceedings, and that hon. gentleman used language which, I am glad to say, has been peculiar to himself and has not been adopted generally by hon. members on the other side of the House. But he has nothing whatever to say about the action of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, for whom I have great respect, said at a ban-

quet-and it is something for which he ought to be commended-at Montreal, given to Sir Percy Girouard, that he would not tolerate any interference with the militia even by a colleague, and that the interference of a colleague, or of any person politically, would sap the very foundations ' of the militia system. I am sorry to say that the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence should,have seen fit to have abdicated his functions and delegated his duties to the hon. Minister of Agriculture at the time he knew there was a controversy going on in regard to the formation of this regiment in the eastern townships, in which the hon. Minister of Agriculture was talking a great deal of interest. I say it is an unfortunate thing that the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence should have delegated his functions to that hon. gentleman, knowing the facts of the case, and allowed him to manage his department during his absence. If ' Hansard ' reports him rightly, he said that the trouble could not possibly have occurred if he had been present at the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I am sura the hon. gentleman will allow me once more to correct that statement. I said nothing of the kind. I said that if I had been in Ottawa at the time that the organization of the corps in the eastern townships was commenced I would have consulted my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, and that probably this trouble would not have occurred.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I do not wish to misrepresent the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence, but I think that what he has said virtually bears out the statement 1 made. I simply wish to convey this fact to the minds of hon. members that he did say something to the effect that if he had been present during the organization of the corps this unfortunate trouble would not have occurred. It is extremely to be regretted that it did occur, and I simply wish to emphasize the feeling of the militia corps generally throughout the country, that Dord Dundonald was the best officer we ever had, and that the militia has suffered a great disadvantage as the result of his removal. What Is to be regretted still further-perhaps this is not exactly the time to make statements of this kind, but I had not an opportunity of taking part In the two debates that took place in the House-is the summary and unceremonious manner of the dismissal of Dol'd Dundonald. We know very well that all through this unfortunate incident very scant courtesy has been shown that brilliant soldier, and that in no way has the government recognized the services that he has rendered to this country. I was surprised to hear the hon. Minister of Finance speak so positively on the strength of what had been said by Mr. Winston Churchill in the British House of Commons of the Conservative party exploiting Dord Dundonald. I have looked in vain in the speeches of hon.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
gentlemen on the other side of the House to-day to find any evidence in confirmation of that statement. In the city of Toronto, as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has said, there was not a word of political significance uttered by any of those who made speeches there, and if the government are inclined to take what Dord Dundonald has said in his own defence, and very rightly said, as evidence of his acting with the Conservative party, it is their business. There has been no effort, as far as 1 can learn, or as far as I have seen, to exploit Dord Dundonald. He is quite capable of taking care of himself in every sense of the word, but it is to be most deeply regretted that we have lost the services of this gentleman to the militia force, and I cannot reiterate that statement too often. Many things have been said of Lord Dundonald of a very derogatery character by the press of the country and by hon. gentlemen on the government side of the House, and it is not to be wondered at that he should take the very first opportunity of defending himself, as he did most effectually in the city of Toronto. Horn, gentlemen may have remembered not very long ago the accident which happened in New York, by which a very large number of people were drowned on the ' General Slocum,' and that afterwards reference was made to one of the ballads of Colonel John Hay, who is now, I think, Secretary of State of the United States government. It was referred to in this way, that in the fact of the engineer having died at his post, another ' Jim Bludso ' had been found. There is another poem of Colonel John Hay, which hon. gentlemen supporting the government might take to heart in connection with this very Dundonald incident. It is a little ballad devoted to the remarks of Sergeant Tilmon Joy, to the committee of white men in a western town who had got together and passed resolutions expelling a nigger. I will give you one of the verses, so that you can see the application :
I reckon I git your drift, gents,-
You 'low the boy shan't stay ;
This is a Whiteman's country ;
You's Dimocrafs, you say ;
And whereas, and seein', and wherefore, The times bein' all out o' j'int,
The nigger has got to mosey From the limits of Spunky P'int !
Le's reason the thing a minute ;
I'm an old-fashioned Dimocrat too, Though I laid my politics out o' the way For to keep till the war was through. But I come hack here, allowin'
To vote as I used to do,
Though it gravels me like the devil to train
Along o' sich fools as you.
Now gentlemen, there was no Tilmon Joy found in the Liberal cabinet when in that very unceremonious way, not a nigger, but a gentleman and a soldier, was expelled from the limits of Canada. There was not one found amongst the Liberal ministers

would, stand up for Lord Dundonald and prevent his expulsion from this country. They all with one accord held up their hands for that magnificent Order in Council to absolve the Minister of Agriculture from any wrong doing-although they said in the document itself that these statements regarding the Minister of Agriculture were un-necessry to the record. They passed their Order in Council and sent it forth to the country, and the General Officer Commanding was expelled without one voice being raised in his favour in that cabinet council of Liberal ministers. I can tell hon. gentleman opposite, that they will find when they appeal to the country, that there will he a good many Sergeant Tilmon Joys in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I desire to say a few words on this question, not for the purpose of discussing the militia, hut to repudiate as a Conservative, the imputation that the Conservative party has been using the Dundonald incident, or Lord Dundonald himself for political purposes. I assert, that if it had come to the knowledge of the Conservative party, that the Minister of Agriculture had interfered and meddled with the appointments to the 13th Scottish Light Dragoons as we now know he did, we would have taken the course we have taken whether Lord Dundonald had been a,t the head of the militia or not. No matter who the man might have been who was the General Officer Commanding, the position we took would have been taken, and would have been persisted in as we intend to persist in it. I go further and say, that if Lord Dundonald had condoned the action of the Minister of Agriculture, if he had been silent on the subject and the matter had come to our knowledge, we would have taken this same action, regardless of Lord Dundonald or his opinion. The point is, not what Lord Dundonald thinks or does not think, but the interests and welfare of the militia of Canada, and the absolute necessity now and at all times to prevent such political interference with appointments to the militia as that which we have been condemning. I object to the language of the Finance Minister when he speaks of this as a Dundonald question. It is not a Dundonald question as regards this House or as regards this country. It might more properly be called a Fisher question ; but above all it is a militia question, and a question of the non-interference of politicians with the militia. That is the question before the House. I object to the Minister of Finance charging the Conservative party with using Lord Dundonald for political purposes. The Conservative party has never thought of such a thing, and I can assure hon. gentlemen opposite, that the Conservative party as a party are not quite such fools as to treat the question in that manner. The matter is a very serious one;
it has gone to the hearts and will stay in the hearts of the people of this country, and we would only weaken the attack we have made and will continue to make upon the government, by treating it as a personal question relating to the gentleman who happened to be the Commander in Chief at the moment. I want to say a word as to a quotation made by the Minister of Finance. I do so because in apparently making a quotation he has used language conveying a very different signification from what appears in the paragraph he was reading from. The report in the paper says :
No representation had been made by the government of Canada, which was able to take care of itself.
That is a very simple statement indeed ; a commonplace remark; that the government of Canada is able to take care of itself. Let us see how the Minister of Finance turned it, or I would say twisted it, in order to give it a different meaning. These are his exact words, I have obtained them :
But there are other matters in which no such aid is needed, and this unhappy Dundonald business is one of that kind. Mr. Arnold Foster very correctly stated, and it is perhaps the point in his observations which we appreciate most that this is a matter in which the Canadian government have shown that they are well able to deal with it themselves.
That is a very different thing from the report of what Mr. Foster said, as it ap-appears in the newspapers. The Minister of Finance uses language that would convey to the people of Canada, that Mr. Arnold Foster has approved of the past action of the government of Canada in this matter, that the government of Canada in what they have done have shown that they were well able to deal with it themselves. Why does the Minister of Finance want to turn the words ; why did he not use the exact words in the newspaper report ? why did he want to use Mr. Arnold Foster as apparently approving of the action that the Canadian government had taken in this matter ? The Minister of Finance had the exact words before him, and I object to his wrong interpretation of the words of Mr. Arnold Foster, -which interpretation is as far from being the truth, as is the statement that we are using Lord Dundonald for political purposes. The Minister of Finauce went out of his way to pay a compliment to Mr. Lloyd George. He said :	[DOT]
Mr. Lloyd George, I am bound to speak of as one of the most distinguished members of the imperial parliament.
Well, I think most of us know something of Mr. Lloyd George, and we know that if he is distinguished for anything it is for his extreme political opinions. He is distinguished as being one of the small party that were known in England as the pro-Boer party ; a party which would never have

sent a soldier to South Africa if they had had their way. Mr. Lloyd George is a gentleman who would have withdrawn the British flag from South Africa if he had had his way, and this is the gentleman the Minister of Finance belauds here as if he were one of the greatest men in England There is a rather significant paragraph in this paper which was not read.
Mr. Lloyd George spoke of ' the pain this controversy would cause Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who, as was truly said, was one of the staunchest friends of the empire at the time of its great struggle.' Well, those who know Mr. Lloyd George know perfectly well that the man he would call the staunchest friend of the British empire 5n that great struggle would be a man holding his own opinions as to submission to the Boers ; and I doubt very much whether the First Minister of Canada will take it as a compliment that that remark has fallen from Mr. Lloyd George. If the hon. Finance Minister wants to stand on the same footing as Mr. Lloyd George does, he will accept that compliment; but I think there are few men in this Dominion who would want to stand in the same shoes as Mr. Lloyd George does with regard to South Africa.
Now, Sir, when we took up this question in this House, I was under the impression, as I think most gentlemen on this side were that we were doing our duty as members of the opposition. We were criticising one of the departments of government. We had heard of certain things that were being done in the administration or non administration of the Militia Department that ought to be condemned, regardless of the source from which the information came, except that we knew the facts stated to be true. We condemned what had been done. Was that not our duty ? What would be the object of our sitting here as an opposition if we were to allow such a matter as that to pass uncondemned when we were considering the Militia Department? For what purpose are we here ? We criticise and condemn the railway administration. Are we exploiting somebody when we do that ? We took up the Grand Trunk Pacific matter a year ago and criticised it and condemned it, and we had the assistance of Hon. Mr! Blair in doing so. Were we exploiting Mr. Blair ? Surely the fact that Mr. Blair happened to join us in our condemnation of the government was not an exploitation of Mr. Blair by the opposition. Nor is the fact that we happened to think and speak about the Militia Department as Lord Dundonald did, an exploitation by us of that eminent soldier for party purposes. Our view of the misconduct of the hon. Minister of Agriculture in meddling with the militia has nothing whatever to do with the General Officer Commanding. We have exploited-as apparently we want to use that word so much in this House-the Treadgold Commission,

maintopic: SUPPLY-INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
and with some effect; but I do not know that in doing that, we exploited any particular gentleman connected with it. We have been taking up the Audit Department. Was that exploiting Mr. McDougall ? Surely we can take up and- discuss and criticise a department without acting for or using a particular Individual who happens, to be connected with it. _ Now, I object to the Finance Minister trying to sidetrack this question by diverting the attention of the public from the conduct of the hon. Minister of Agriculture and that of the hon. Minister of Militia to Lord Dundonald. Lord Dundonald can defend himself. We do not attempt to defend him here. It is not our business to do so. Our business is to criticise hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to the conduct of the affairs entrusted to them, and we generally do so, no matter who the man may be who may be helped or hurt by our criticism.

Before six o'clock, Mr Speaker, I was referring to the action of the opposition in the House with regard to the question under discussion as it affected the militia, and I ask what could the opposition have done when it learned what had been attempted with regard to the Scottish Dragoons, other than it did.
