If there has been any exploiting, who has been guilty of it ? Did the Conservative party exploit the Montreal banquet ? I think not. I do not think that any hon. gentleman on the other side would pretend for one moment that the Conservative party any more than the Liberal party, had anything to do with or any knowledge of that banquet, before it took place. Did we exploit the publishing of the proceedings at that banquet in the press ? I think not.
It is not even pretended mat we did. Did we exploit the minister's letter demanding from the General Officer Commanding an explanation of what occurred at that meet-

ing ? Certainly not. Nor did we exploit the publication in the press of that correspondence. We took no part in it. It all took place without any interference of the Conservative opposition. I do not believe, Sir, that anybody will question that statement. The incident arose entirely outside of the Conservative party. Whatever interference there was before the matter was brought to the attention of this House came from the Liberal party alone. When the facts came before us, we condemned the Minister of Agriculture for his interference and meddling. We condemned that minister who, not content, Mr. Speaker, with the plough-share, wanted to don the sword as well; who. not content with the management of one department of the government, which certainly should exercise all the qualities he possesses, undertook to interfere with and control another department with which constitutionally he had nothing to do. Nor was it a mere temporary interference with the departmental functions and duties of his colleagues. No, this had been going on for months. It began in the early days, almost at the very inception of the organization of this regiment. We find, as was shown in the discussion in this House, that from the very beginning the Minister of Militia was almost ignored in this matter. From the very outset, the Minister of Agriculture was interviewed by the officers and by everybody interested in the formation of that dragoon regiment. They came to him as if they were dealing with something affecting the experimental farm. They never went near the Minister of Militia, and one would have wondered why they went to the one gentleman and not the other, had not political developments been brought to light, had we not found that the Minister of Agriculture was interfering, not because he' had more experience in militia matters than his colleague, but because his own political interests were involved. It was for this reason alone he interfered in this matter and took it entirely out of the hands of his colleague, the Minister of Militia, who, I regret to say, calmly submitted to the interference. And indeed there can be very little doubt that the Minister of Militia went out of the way at a convenient moment in order to give his colleague full swing and let him deal with this matter to suit his own political purposes. He dealt with it, not in the interests of the militia, but in the interests of his political party-a party of course which would not think of exploiting such a thing as a regiment of dragoons or any other regiment for party purposes. That, Sir, was the position under which the matter came before this House, and we dealt with it in that light. We had some notable words -from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), words
that we could find no fault with. He said, as reported at page 4582 of ' Hansard ':
No political consideration should be allowed to interfere.
Well, Sir, there is nobody on this side of the House who will dispute that, for it coincides exactly with our own view ; and, if the hon. gentleman had only practised what he professed, there would have been no discussion upon this subject in Canada, there would have been no discussion upon it in the British House of Commons, nor should we have had all this turmoil and trouble over the question of the General Officer Commanding, who, probably, had it not been for the course pursued by hon. gentlemen opposite, would have been General Officer Commanding to-day and would have continued in that position for some years to come. What is the fact ? In the face of these good professions of the hon. gentleman that no political interference should be allowed to interfere, we find the true state of things explained at page 12 of the papers brought down by the government, in which the colonel of the regiment who speaks at peril of his commission,-so that, I think, we can accept every word of what he says as certainly not going beyond the truth-puts the facts in this form :
Mr. Fisher objected to him

That is, to the proposed major of the regiment.
-for no other reason than that he was a strong political opponent of his, and was quite determined to block the whole organization unless Dr. Pickel's name w7as withdrawn.
That, Sir, is the fact. That is the way the hon. Minister of Agriculture acts in the fact of his profession, put on ' Hansard ' that ' no political considerations should be allowed to interfere.' And yet we are charged with using for political puiposes this question that has been brought before the House and before the country in such a manner. I would like to ask hon. gentlemen opposite what is to be the result of this sort of thing if it goes on. If we are to have militia ti'ained on political lines, where are these regiments and the officei's who command them to find themselves placed ? Will the colonel of the regiment sit at his mess table, and ai-range all the good grits on his right hand and on his left aiil the bad Tories ; or if the other party happens to be in power the Conservatives on the right and the Grits on the left ? And when the question arises of which soldier is to be raised from the ranks and made a coi'poral, is the first question to be considered what his politics may be ? Are they to consider whether he is a good party man or an indifferent party man ? Are they to consider, when they are making a man a sergeant, whether he has done his whole duty as a politician, or whether, perhaps, he has a cousin, or a nephew,

7163
or a brother, who happens to be on the opposite side ? Are these the considerations that are to be taken up whenever anything is to be done for the militia ? And yet, that would be the inevitable result of the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture, and the conduct of the Minister of Militia in submitting to this uncalled for and unconstitutional dictation. That most unfortunate conduct of ministers led to the speech made at the banquet at Montreal. Sir, I do not care whether that speech was an indiscretion or not. There have been many indiscreet things done that 'have resulted in good ; and, however, indiscreet Lord Dundonald may have been-and we need not enter into the discussion of that here-I trust and believe that the conduct of the Minister of Agriculture in this matter will result in great good to the militia of Canada, for the outcry against his interference on this occasion will put down, once for all, any desire of a minister, no matter to what party he may belong, to ever again interfere in such a manner with the appointments in the militia.
I do not care to pursue that subject further ; we discussed it pretty fully when it was before the House, and for my part I think it ought to have been left there. But was it left there ? After we had discussed the question in this House, was it ended ? And, if it did not end, who continued it ? Was it the Conservative party? I think not. Who was it made attacks, after the discussion in this House, upon Lord Dundonald ? Did not we find the whole Liberal press filled with the attacks on the General Officer, charging him with political intent, charging him with incompetency, and reflecting upon him in every possible manner ? Why, I think the Minister of Militia went so far as to question the English used by the Earl of Dundonald. There was nothing that they did not say. Was that exploiting the Dundonald incident ? Was that continuing the Dundonald question and using Lord Dundonald for political purposes ? I do not care whether they used it for attack upon their opponents or for their own defence, the men who pursued that policy used the Dundonald incident for political purposes. And hon. gentlemen opposite, and not the Conservatives, are the guilty parties. But there was more, Sir. Who furnished to the Liberal papers information that was contained only in private or suppressed reports ? Who conveyed to the Toronto ' Globe ' information on which to base charges that Lord Dundonald had made extravagant demands on this country ? Was that exploiting this incident on behalf of the Conservative party or was it exploiting it on behalf of hon. gentlemen opposite ? I think they were carrying on the warfare on political lines when they were acting in this way. Was not the attack upon Lord Dundonald in nearly every Liberal organ ? And, when Lord Dundonald was asked up Mr. BARKER.
to Toronto to address the people, was he to go there and be silent with regard to the [ matter on which he had been attacked ? Were hon. gentlemen to be given the opportunity to say that Lord Dundonald, by silence, admitted what was charged against him ? These hon. gentleman would have been delighted if only Lord Dundonald had held his tongue. They would have come out next morning and said : Lord Dundonald dared not deny the charges they made. And as to the people who asked him to speak is it to be supposed that the ladies and gentlemen of Toronto who went by the thousand to receive him, expected to listen to a lecture on cavalry tactics or to a reading of the latest edition of his work upon drill ? What did they go for ? Why, the question was red hot in the country, Lord Dundonald being the hero of it ; and these people went to hear what Lord Dundonald had to say in his own defence against the attacks that the Liberal papers were making upon him. That is what they went for, and there was not a man or woman in that hall in Toronto who would not have been disappointed if he had left unsaid the things he said-there is no question about that. It is absurd for hon. gentlemen opposite to say that Lord Dundonald took advantage of the position. Why, it would have been sheer nonsense to ask such a man to go from Ottawa to Toronto to address five or six thousand people In Massey Hall and yet say nothing on the only subject in which they were interested. And are we to suppose, do hon. gentlemen opposite suppose, that the people of Toronto are so unintelligent that they do not appreciate the proprieties? Do the gentlemen opposite suppose that the reception which the general met with on that occasion did not show clearly where the hearts of the people were on the subject ? Do they suppose that the acclamations with which he was received meant nothing ? Do they suppose that when the people of Toronto took the horses from his carrriage and dragged it to the station they did not endorse everything he did and said ? Does it mean nothing w-hen a man receives in Toronto, the chief city of Ontario, the grandest reception that any man ever received there? And yet hon. gentlemen say he is being exploited for political purposes. I can understand how he might have been exploited. I know that if only 400 or 500 people had gone to that meeting he would have been exploited for the Liberal party. The difficulty is that it was a grand success, that the people showed their sympathy with the man. The whole difficulty lies there :	it was not that
he went to the reception, it was the fact that he carried the people with him and that he made it plain that he has got the heart and sympathy of every man in Canada. I'do not care whether you speak of the incident as regards Quebec, as

regards Ontario, or as regards any other province. I believe that Lord Dundonald today could go into any county in Quebec or in any other province in this country and meet with as good a reception as he met with in Toronto. It is absolute nonsense to say that Lord Dondonald was seeking a political result.	I believe that there are
few men within sound of my voice who know what Lord Dunuonald's politics are. For my own part I do not know ; I never heard what they are, and I do not think any one here can give me that information. Lord Dundonad cares no more about the politics of Canada than he does about the politics of Australia or New Zealand. He is a British subject and soldier, who is here for one purpose, to do good for the militia of Canada. That is his sole purpose and whether Conservatives are in power or Liberals are in power is a matter of absolute indifference to him. Nobody can question that, and I venture to say that if a Conservative government had been in power and the Conservative minister had done what the present ministers did, Lord Dundonald would have acted in precisely j the way he did, Mr. Speaker, I should [ have liked to have heard the denunciations of hon. gentlemen opposite if in such an event they had been sittiug on this side of the House. It would be a treat to hear the First Minister get up and denounce as an outrage upon the people of this country that an officer sent here to command the militia should be treated in such a manner for political purposes. Had a Conservative minister of Agriculture taken advantage of his position to meddle in the organization of a militia regiment, and to prevent the giving of a commission to a political opponent to a reputable man simply because he happened to be a Liberal, what an outcry we would have had ! If the First /Minister could only come over here and make such a speech for us it would be worth reading a dozen times over. But it is the other way around, and hon. gentlemen opposite look upon it in another light. The Minister of Agriculture is allowed to interfere, to intrude upon a matter with which lie has nothing to do. and to do more mischief to the cause of the militia of Canada than he can do good in his agricultural department if he lives a century. I have served, in my time in all ranks in the militia from private up to commanding a company.
I can carry my mind a great many j years back and in all my time, until this intrusion of the Minister of Agriculture. I never heard of political interference in the militia. I know. Sir, that in the city of -which I have the honour to be one of the representatives, we have an old regiment, the 13th of Hamilton, which is a credit to the country. That regiment for years was j commanded under the Conservative government by a Liberal Colonel, a Liberal of the 1 Liberals, the present Attorney General of
Ontario, and I say to his credit that
I do not believe that in all the many years that he commanded the regiment there was ever a question on his part or on the part of any officer of his regiment
(as to whether an applicant for a commission was a Liberal or Conservative. The ..great difficulty in these cases is to get the men who can afford to take the positions, t can understand thoroughly the position of the people down in Sweetsburg. In Hamilton, where perhaps we have at our command more men of means than they have at Sweetsburg, the trouble is to get men who will assume the expense, and it is rather a favour to a regiment than otherwise for a young man to accept a commission. A new regiment has recently been formed, a Scottish regiment too, and I can only say that I hope and believe it will always have as excellent a reputation as the old 13th for freedom from party politics. I know too that in the battery of artillery that has been for many years a credit to the city of Hamilton, there wore under a Conservative government, four Liberals and only one Conservative officer and I have been assured by * gentlemen connected with that battery they never heard one word as to the political leaning of any man holding a commission in it. I think that what I know of Hamilton is the case in Toronto and throughout the province of Ontario, and I have yet to learn that there is any other condition in the province of Quebec. I believe that the same spirit has actuated the people of the province of Quebec and that it has remained for the Minister of Agriculture to endeavour to start a new order of things and to intrude politics into the militia to affect, perhaps, the chances of the return of some particular man to the local legislature or to the House of Commons.

I would not interpose to prolong the discussion of this matter, which to my mind is a most unfortunate affair, both in the interests of Canada itself and in its relations to the British empire, but for the fact that there is involved in this discussion a principle which is of the utmost importance not only to Canadians but to British subjects throughout the world. It involves to my mind a principle which is being unwarrantably violated by the government of the day. The principle to which I refer is this : Shall a British subject in any part of the British domain be denied that privilege which we all claim to enjoy-the right of free thought and free speech ? I do not believe that in Canada such a sentiment as that, the denial of free thought, and free speech will be tolerated by the people. I do not believe it would be tolerated in any other part of the British empire and it is because this principle is involved that I take this occasion to offer a few remarks upon the question of the dismissal of Lord Dun-



donald and the action of the government in connection therewith. Prior to the speech made by Lord Dundonald in Toronto I concede that the matter was fairly treated and might be fairly treated as a matter of etiquette as between himself and the government under whom he was serving, but once the government had satisfied itself by wrecking its vengeance on Lord Dundonald by the summary dismissal of that gentleman from its service he ceased to be under the control of this government and as a free born British subject he was entitled to speak as he did speak in the city of Toronto. He was, as my hon. friend says, after his dismissal by the government an elector of the Dominion of Canada entitled to all the rights and privileges appertaining to a British subject in this country.
I want just for a moment to contrast the action of the government in its dealings with Lord Dundonald with its action in its dealings with another and as celebrated an individual but one who is not celebrated upon the same lines. The offence charged against Lord Dundonald was an act of indiscretion. It was charged that he was guilty of a breach of etiquette as between himself and the government and without calling upon Lord Dundonald to justify himself or make his defence before this government or before the country he was summarily dismissed as every hon. gentleman in this House knows and as the country knows full well. He was not offered the privilege of any ordinary British subject, not possessing the merit that Lord Dundonald has won. of making his defence. He was not accorded the privilege which is offered to the ordinary criminal of the land of making amends for his first offence by trying to do better. He was not offered the opportunity of retracting what he had said and endeavouring by his conduct in the future to satisfy the government of the day and to satisfy its requirements in regard to his position. He was a man as full of honours as he was full of years. A young man though he may be, I venture to say that the honours which have been heaped upon him as a result of the service which he has rendered to his country very much predominate, override and overshadow anything that lias occurred during the few years he has spent here. I venture to say right here that the name of Lord Dundonald, although he may have been discredited by this government, will be held in honour and in reverence by the people of Canada and of the British empire when this government has gone down in disgrace. But, Sir, let me refer to the analogy that I spoke of a moment ago. We have in the service of the government today another man who has a history in Canada. He is not the hero of Ladysmith. He is not the man who had the courage to lead our Canadian boys to victory in South Africa. He is not the man who had the courage to take his life in his hand td de-Mr. PORTER.
fend the British empire. He is the man who went throughout the length and breadth of Canada to do dirty nefarious, political election tricks and was afterwards appointed to' the position that he now occupies in Great Britain. T refer to Mr. W. T. R. Preston. There is this difference between the two gentlemen that I speak of : One, Lord Dundonald, full of honour ; the other, W. T. R. Preston, practically driven from Canada by dishonour. How does the government treat these two men ? The man who would command the respect of this government, who would command the respect of the people of this country is cast out and discredited. Mr. W. T. R. Preston is given a position of emolument, a position of profit, an important position under this government and not only that, but, Sir, he is guilty of the very same offence, if it may be considered an offence, that Lord Dundonald has been charged with by this government. During the discussion of this very matter and since Lord Dundonald's case has come before the government, Mr. W. T. R. Preston has taken occasion to write a letter to the public press. What for ? For the purpose of defending Lord Dundonald ?-no, For the purpose of defending the British people ?-no. For the purpose of the business for which he is employed ?-no ; but, for the purpose of defending this government that he felt was in need of defence. When he was guilty of that indiscretion what did this government do ? Did it say to Mr. Preston as it said to Lord Dundonald : You have been guilty of a grave indiscretion and off comes your head without a defence ?-no, no ; not at all. When it found out that he had been guilty of an act of indiscretion and when the matter was pressed home to this government very strongly, so strongly that it felt it must do something, what did it do ? The government wrote home and told him that he must not do it again, that it would give him another chance. I am reminded of the fact that his salary is to be increased this year. Perhaps this is the reward for his activity in serving the government in this way. This is only one instance of the way in which this government has treated Lord Dundonald in comparison with the way in which it has treated gentlemen in its employ who are favourable to it. I do not mean to have the House infer from this that Lord Dundonald is unfavourable to the government. I do not believe that Lord Dundonald is unfavourable to the government. I believe that Lord Dundonald by every expression he has given utterance to since this matter has come before the people and by his acts during the time he was employed in the administration of military affairs in this country, has shown that he is not unfavourable to this government, that he is not unfavourable to this opposition, but that he is favourable to

the whole people of Canada and that he is true to the British empire. So, I think it is paltry, it is low, it is mean for any one to charge Lord Dundonald with being unfavourable to either one political party or the other. High as our political standard may be, Lord Dundonald looks to a still higher standard ; his object is that of a true patriot. I wish to call attention to another matter, and I make reference to it particularly because it occurred in the riding I have the honour to represent, and it illustrates as forcibly as can be illustrated, the honesty and the integrity of Lord Dundonald and the high purpose of the man. It proves that he was not actuated or influenced by political, or any but the highest motives. Lord Dundonald spoke of this matter in his speech at Toronto, and the facts are these. Shortly after Lord Dundonald took office in this country, Lieutenant-Colonel Ponton, of Belleville, a gentleman who occupies in the riding I represent, and in the entire district in which he lives, a reputation that might be the envy of any man. Colonel Ponton comes from military stock ; his great grandfather, his grandfather, and his father had the privilege of occupying the positions of colonels or lieutenant-colonels in the British army. He is a military man from start to finish. He commenced his service in the Queen's Own, passed to the 15th Argyle Light Infantry of Hastings and ultimately became commander of that regiment. After a long and honourable service in the militia, lie was retired retaining rank. After his retirement from the service, at a citizen's banquet which was in no way concerned with military affairs, Colonel Ponton was asked to respond to the toast of the army and navy, on account of his long service in our active militia. He took occasion to point out some of the weaknesses of the present administration, in conducting militia affairs. I have Colonel Ponton's own word for it, that within three days after he made the speech, he had a letter from the department here demanding to know whether he had used these expressions or not. Colonel Ponton is a man of the stamp of Lord Dundonald, and his answer to the .department was: I did give expression to these opinions, I am a retired officer, I was exercising my right as a British subject, and I refuse to withdraw a single word I uttered. What was the result ? It has only come to Ilnght since the Dundonald matter has been under discussion. As an appendix to that letter, he said to the minister : Having answered your question I demand to know who has made this charge against me, and in what way I have violated my duty ? That letter was handed over to Lord Dundonald with the request from the department, that he should recommend the dismissal of Colonel Ponton, but what did Lord Dundonald do ? He refused to allow political exigencies to 228j
interfere with the proper administration of the militia of Canada, and as Lord Dundonald told us in Toronto, he ordered the correspondance to be pigeon-holed, and Colonel Ponton still occupies his position as a retired colonel of the 15th Argyle Light Infantry and this government did not have the courtesy or courage to answer iCol. Ponton's demand. But this is not all. During the time that controversy was going on between the government and Lord Dundonald, there was a correspondence between Lord Dundonald and a most honourable gentleman who at one time occupied the most prominent position in Canada, and who is to-day honorary colonel of the Argyle Light Infantry, and the action of Colonel Ponton upon that occasion was justified by that gentleman, and Lord Dundonald's action also upheld. And Sir, I have not the slightest fear that when the investigation that is mooted-I was going to say ordered-when the investigation comes that will probably take place in regard to Lord Dundonald's action in this country ; when the evidence comes to be sifted in the old country after his return, I have no doubt whatever that Lord Dundonald will be able to answer satisfactorily the charges made against him, and to confute those who are opposed to him. I have every confidence that Lord Dundonald will be able to acquit himself honourably at home as he has already honourably acquitted himself in Canada. And, what is the charge made against Lord Dundonald ? They say he has been guilty of an act of indiscretion, but the real fact is that the charge against him amounts to an indictment that Lord Dundonald told the truth, a thing which is entirely antagonistic to the principle of this government. Lord Dundonald endeavoured to the best of Ms ability, in the report which he signed and presented to the government, to bring before the people and parliament of Canada the things that were necessary to put our militia force on a proper footing. After he had exhausted, as he says himself, every reasonable means of gaining redress, he was driven, on account of the political interference with the establishment of the 13th Scottish Dragoons, to give public expression to his utterances at the Montreal banquet. There was no other alternative left, and we can but praise the man who had the courage to sacrifice his own chances of advancement for the purpose, not of helping the government or the opposition, but for the purpose of benefiting the whole Dominion of Canada. Reference has been made to publications in the press of Great Britain, dealing with this Dundonald incident. I have had placed in my hands to-night the latest reports in regard to that matter, and as the search light is turned on, and the British people begin to understand the true inwardness of the affair, public opinion becomes more and more in accord with Lord Dundonald. Let me read to the House a state-

ment In a cablegram published in the Montreal ' Star ' to-night :
Winston Churchill although attacking Lord Dundonald admitted that the allegations he made were probably only too true.
Mr. Arnold Poster, Secretary of War, said he pronounced no opinion upon the merit or demerit of Lord Dundonald's action, before Lord Dundonald had been heard in his own defence.
The British government would not, condemn a man before he was heard, but I am sorry to say this Canadian government has been guilty of that offence.
The ' Morning Post ' says :
His offence was a splendid indiscretion in a case in which position and reputation were risked to serve the public interest.
To my mind that fairly expresses the sentiment of the people of Canada, Lord Dundonald has made a sacrifice for the people of Canada, and I doubt not that when the time comes

and it "cannot come too soon-the people of Canada will show at the polls that they uphold Lord Dundonald, and that they uphold the Conservative party who uphold him, by defeating the government which has without just cause or excuse inflicted this great and unjust punishment upon this patriotic soldier of the empire.

No, coal and wood are charged to public buildings on the farms as elsewhere. That has been done ever since the establishment of the farm and it was the same under the regime which the hon. gentleman supported before 1890 as it is to-day. Exactly the same system was adopted and exactly the same charges were made in 1896 as to-day. The results are identically the same. The explanation of the difference which the hon. gentleman attempted to show which at the time I gave in general terms, I have now given in exact detail, and it fully sustains

what I said then. The hon. gentleman went on to talk about a number of other things connected with my department. I shall not go into the details as I said a few minutes ago. I am going to deal with the question on broad principles only. The hon. gentleman went on to speak about the census. I am surprised after what occurred last session in this House that the hon. gentleman or any of his friends should bring up that question. There was a motion introduced during the last session of this House upon which that question was thoroughly discussed, a motion which hon. gentlemen opposite moved on going into supply of censure upon this government, and especially upon the Minister of Agriculture in regard to the compiling of the census. I then showed very clearly what the result of that census was and the House was so satisfied with what I showed that it voted down by one of the largest majorities that a Liberal government ever had In this House, the motion of hon. gentlemen opposite. I freely admit that it did cost a great deal more than the censuses which hon. gentlemen opposite took in 1891 and 1881, but, Sir, I also showed and I was able to prove to a demonstration that the census of 1901 was an accurate census, was a census which gave full information in regard to the statistics of this country, whereas the census of 1891 was a census which was not only full of inaccuracies, but was full of deception and deceit and which went before the people of the country and showed falsehood and deceit on almost every line and page. I venture to say that it is far better for the people and far more to the credit of the government to be able to show true and accurate statistics of this country than to show inaccurate and false statistics even if the true statistics do require a little more money to get. It is easy enough to compile a census in the way in which the census of 1891 was compiled. It is easy enough to bring down schedule after schedule and inaccurately and carelessly compile them, but it is a different thing altogether to take these schedules and go over them and check them and go over them again and see that they are accurate. I need not go into that question as I did last year. I need not point out that in the whole of the province of Quebec while the census of the land area was taken in arpents and the census of the crops was taken in minots when the schedules came to be compiled in Ottawa the minots were written as bushels and the arpents were written as acres with the result that the whole province of Quebec made a poorer showing in its production than any other part of the Dominion. This is only one of the hundreds of specimens of the way in which the census of 1891 Mr. FISHER.
was compiled. It is easy enough to make compilations of that kind but if the census had been properly and accurately compiled I venture to say that it would have cost more than the census of 1901. I do not for a moment shrink from taking credit for the fact that upon the census of 1901 we have spent enough money to make it an accurate and true census of the statistics of Canada, not such a census as the census of 1891 was, and which has gone abroad to the country and to the world as misrepresenting the people of Canada, misrepresenting their numbers, misrepresenting their industries, misrepresenting their productions in a way that is a shame and a disgrace to the people who compiled that census and who are responsible for its taking.
The hon. gentleman has gone on to speak in regard to some other branches of my department. He spoke about the cheese curing rooms. He said that I have inaugurated some experiments in regard to improvements in cheese curing. That is quite true. I glory in the fact. I am willing to take all the credit or all the disgrace connected with that fact. It is true that a few years ago the quality of our cheese was being criticised on the English market because of the condition in which it arrived in Great Britain. It is true that a certain unevenness of quality was remarked and that we investigated the reasons so as to ascertain whether it was due to the fact that our cheese was not cured at the proper temperature to make it as good as it could be made. We had discussed this question with the cheese-makers in the country. Prof. Robertson, myself and other officers of the department had gone to the great dairy conventions of the country and had discussed the question as to what ought to be done to remedy this evil. We found, as a matter of fact, that the evil was largely if not altogether due to the uneven temperature of the cheese-curing rooms. Then, the question arose :	How
could it be demonstrated that our cheese should be cured in an even temperature ? We discussed it wfth experts. The result was that w'e established large central curing rooms. There was no use in carrying on experiments of this kind on a small scale by which a few cheese might be cured here and there. It was necessary to cure enough to show that this method was the proper one to remedy the defect which then existed. WTe did that. These central curing rooms cost a good deal of money. The hon. gentleman has given a lot of figures which I cannot dispute. I have not the figures under my hand necessary to do so. I will have to take the hon. gentleman's figures as being correct which is rather a large supposition when the hon. gentleman refers to figures in this House.

The hon. gentleman must know, if lie lias studied the question, that the result of the cool curing has been an absolute success ; that the cheese so cured brings a higher price and that the people who handle that cheese in the English market, our only market for the export of cheese, prefer it and pay a higher price for it than for the ordinary cheese. I shall not go into any lengthy details, but I will point out, that during the present session the cool-cured cheese sold in the markets of St. Hyacinthe, Cowansville, Brockville and Woodstock. On June 9th, in Brockville the board price of cheese was eight cents, but every cheese that came out of the government cool-curing rqom sold for from 8 3-16ths -to 84 cents. On June lOth, the ruling price was 8 cents, and the price of the cool-cured cheese was 8 3-16, 81 and 84 cents. On June 23rd at Brockville, the cool-cured cheese commanded 7f and 7 11-lGths cents as against 7} cents for the ordinary cheese. This shows that buyers appreciate the superiority of the cool-cured cheese and are willing to pay more for it. On June 27th, the board price was eight cents, and again the cool-cured cheese sold for 84, 81 and 8 3-1G cents. There is another remarkable illustration of this. There was a factory near Brockville which had not access to the cool-curing room because it had already all the work it could do. That factory went to the manager and said :	If you allow us to bring
our cheese to the cool-curing room we will not only pay you as usual, but we will treat our cheese ourselves and pay all the expenses of it, because a buyer in Montreal has offered to pay us 1 cent more for our cheese right straight through the season if we can get it cured in the cool-curing room. One of the largest buyers in Montreal considered that cheese cooled in this way at the government station was worth one quarter cent per pound more than the cheese cured in the ordinary factory. I think I have said enough to show that the statement of the hon. gentleman in regard to. the cool-curing rooms is absolutely without foundation. I have shown that the men who are engaged in the business, the buyers in Montreal and in England and that sellers in Canada, appreciate and understand the value this process has been to them, and are prepared to endorse the policy of the government. I may say that during last winter I have had application after application for the establishment of cool-curing rooms all over Ontario, and if the people engaged in the industry were not satisfied with it. they would not have made this application. The statement which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has made is absolutely without foundation and it only shows his ignorance of the cheese industry in this country.
And now as to the poultry industry. I may point out that before these fattening
stations were established it was practically impossible in Canada to get fattened poultry for the table. We were exporting no fattened poultry to Europe, but immediately after the establishment of the fattening stations our poultry exports to Great Britain increased from 818,000 the year before, to over $230,000 the year after. Since that time our exports to England have dropped off, and the reason is that the Canadian market has awakened to the fact that good fattened poultry can be bought in Canada and to-day, Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto. Halifax, Sydney, Hamilton, Guelph and the other cities within reach of these poultry fattening stations absorb the whole output so that they cannot export one pound of poultry, and the supply in fact is not equal to the local demand. The hon. gentleman says that these poultry stations have been expensive. They have been to a certain extent expensive, but it must be remembered that experimental and educational work has been going on at them. It is idle to suppose that an experimental and teaching station would meet the expenses by its output alone.

I know the hon. gentleman thinks he has a Tory hive in Leeds, but I am not afraid in the least to face the hon. gentleman, or any other of his gang, and to meet them on the platform, because I believe that the farmers of Leeds in general are intelligent men. That is rather a difficult thing for one to believe in view of the fact that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has been representing them for so many years. But I still have faith in human nature, and I am led to the conclusion that the constituents of Leeds have not been told the whole truth about public affairs or the hon. gentleman would not represent them in this House. I state emphatically that experimental work is a good investment in the interest of the farmers and agriculturists of this country, even though it should cost more than it gives in money return. I believe that by reason of the experimental work which is being carried on by the gov-

ernment of Canada-a good deal of it carried on before I came into office, more of it carried on since I came into office-as a result of that experimental work to-day the farmers of Canada have at their command a mass of information which is of the utmost utility to them ; a mass of information which is better and more complete than the information which the farmers of any other country on the face of the earth have to aid them in their business.
That is not a boast which is undue or unfounded. It is a boast which I make because of the statements of the people in foreign countries who are coming to Canada for information, for models, for examples as to how best to carry on the work of agriculture. In view of that fact, I venture to say that the trivial criticisms of hon. gentlemen opposite will fall to the ground, and farmers of Canada will support the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in its efforts on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman who has just sat down had adopted throughout the whole of his speech the responsible attitude which he assumed in the last four or five sentences of it, perhaps we would not have so (much reason to complain ; but unfortunately it was only during the last four or five sentences that the hon. gentleman recollected that he was the representative of an 'intelligent and peaceful class of the community, the farmers of Canada. Before that he assumed an attitude which he has been fond of assuming lately, which I venture to say does not very well become him, that is, a belligerent attitude, in which he attempts to intimidate hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. So long as the hon. gentleman assumes the gentle, ladylike attitude which becomes him so well, we have no great reason to complain. The people of the country recognize that in having the hon. .gentleman as a representative of the farming class, they have not exactly a horny-handed son of toil. Still, they are prepared to believe that he is a respectable citizen of Canada, endeavouring, according to the light he possesses, which is not saying very much, to promote the interests of the farmers of Canada.	. ,
But the hon. gentleman has not seen fit to meet the issue and has preferred to bluster and make an unseemly noise. The square issue is this. In his report on the experimental farm on page 429, the hon. minister gives the expenditure for the year ending 30th of .Tune, 1903, -as amounting to $84,128.18. That statement my hon. friend from Leeds has shown to be false and misleading. The true figures are $19,141.66 in excess of that amount. How that expenditure has been divided among the various farms is a matter of no practical interest at present. What we are concerned with is the fact that the total expenditure is over $103,000, whereas the hon. minister in his report puts it down as $84,000. On looking hurriedly at page Y-94 of the Auditor General's Report,, I find various items of expenditure in connection with the Central Farm at Ottawa-not one cent of which is included by the hon. min-minister in his statement, amounting to $8,205.68, showing the total expenditure to be $84,000. Again on turning to page V-112, I find an expenditure, for instance, of $1,430.22 in connection with the Ottawa Experimental Farm not included in his statement, and on the next page, V-113, I find an expenditure of $110.65, which is equally left out. The hon. gentleman has
been compelled to admit that in his statement he deliberately omitted the items, of coal and wood, light, &c.; and I venture to say that if he goes to the riding represented by the hon. member for (Leeds or any other riding in this country, he may speak for hours and will not be able to convince the people that he has any justification for leaving out of the expenditures connected with these farms for coal and wood and other items amounting to over $19,000. Let him speak for any length of time he chooses, he cannot prevent ther coming to the conclusion that any statement which does not include these items is a garbled and dishonest account. Therefore when the hon. minister instead of frankly telling us that he has blundered, tries to excuse himself by saying he has followed the system which was pursued in the old days, he is using an argument which will not commend itself to the people. The question is not what former governments have done, because we are bound to progress, and those who cannot keep pace with the march of progress had better get out and make way for others who can. Let me say to this gentleman, who used to he content with the sickle and the pruning hook, but who now, while he dangles a scythe from his left hand, swings the sword in his right, that it ill becomes him to speak as he has done, and that it would be much better for him to try and, give some reasonable explanation for his conduct. When he speaks, as he has done, of the constituents of my hon. friend from Leeds, as the gang led by that hon. gentleman, let me tell him that his head seems to be swelling larger and larger visibly because forsooth he thinks he has got the better of Lord Dundonald in the petty struggle | which he has forced on that, gentleman, and that when he attempts to decry the people who support such men as my hon. friend from Leeds and other members of the opposition in this House, he will learn perhaps before long that these men will show where their strength lies, and that even with his pruning hook and sword he cannot intimidate the great electorate of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of following the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) in his general argument, but only desire to deal in a genera! way with a matter which has been alluded to, and to which, as I am acquainted with the facts, I feel justified in calling attention. Reference has been made to the poultry stations, and the one established at Holmes-ville has been especially dealt with. Holmes-ville happens to be in my own riding. It is in the centre of a strongly Conservative part of the constituency. Yet I challenge any hon. gentleman on the opposite side to come into the riding of West Huron and attempt to convince the farmers there that the government's expenditure on the poultry station at Holmesville was an unwise or extravagant expendR'we and make a single

vote thereby. While the figures given in the Auditor General's Report show an apparent discrepancy between the receipts and expenditure, they are misleading to this extent, that, unless you know the circumstances, you cannot fairly judge as to the actual results of the work of the station As the bon. minister has said, there was no desire or expectation, in establishing these poultry stations-as is the case with other experimental stations-that they would be iself-susitaininig. But a large number \pf chickens are sold during the year after the Auditor General's Report is closed. If the report was made out to show the receipts for a year of the poultry station's operations, it would show that, except for expenditure on capital account-for buildings and so on -there would toe very little loss. As a result of the work of the station at Holmesville- and I speak only of that, for it is the one with whose work I am familiar-in our section of the country, where we formerly bought chickens at 25 cents and 30 cents a pair the farmers are now selling them, as stated by the hon. minister, at 10 cents per pound. The people have so improved their raising of poultry through the lessons they learned in connection with the poultry station that they are now supplying the local demand at 10 cents per pound-and let me say that they cannot fully supply the demand even at that price. The hon. gentleman may take exception to anything he likes an connection with the Department of Agriculture, hut I challenge him again to take exception in West Huron to the work of the poultry station in that riding. Even the hon. gentleman's Conservative friends endorse it. I know a large number of Conservatives who believe that it has been one of the best institutions ever established under the Department of Agriculture. Men who, at the outset, thought it nothing but an election dodge, are willing to admit that it has been practically useful in the development of the poultry industry.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
Inasmuch as something has been said concerning the poultry stations, and as the station established in the town of Renfrew has been referred to, I shall say a word in defence of it, if defence is required. I d'o not think that any one in the Dominion expects that the experimental farm is going to be an unqualified success financially, and that the balance will invariably be on the right side. But I know that throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion the people are fully satisfied with the work done there. If anything were necessary to prove that fact that proof would be found in the large number of excursions that come to the farm every year from every part of the Dominion of Canada. The farmers come because they expect to learn something, and they go away satisfied because they have learned something. And let me say one word of the work that is being carried on by Professor Saunders Mr. HOLMES.
at that farm. If nothing else had been accomplished by the experimental farm except the successful crossing of wheat and the production of new varieties which will ripen two or three days earlier than others of equal usefulness and value, these experiments alone would make the experimental farm system an unqualified success. These new varieties of wheat will put millions of dollars into the pockets of the farmers of the Northwest, for they are looking for a wheat that will ripen early. The farmers are getting rich every day under the patronage of this government, and that I shall be able to prove. With reference to cool curing of cheese, if there is one thing in relation to the cheese industry which stands out prominently above the others as a marked success, it is the cool curing. If anything were necessary to prove that, I can furnish that proof. It is only a few weeks ago that a deputation of farmers came from the township of Ross to my own town of Renfrew, to the creamery company there, and asked if they could not make arrangements for the cool curing of cheese for the various factories in that section. They said that about twenty factories wanted to bring in cheese and have us cool them and keep them, because we have large cold storage rooms and we could care for the cheese better than they could be cared for elsewhere. They said they could get more for cheese that was cool-cured, and besides there was not the shrinkage that there was under the other system of curing, and they were prepared to give fair remuneration if we would undertake this work for the various factories in that vicinity. And that matter has been taken uip for consideration. What the result may be it is impossible for me to say. Now, with reference to the chicken industry. Of course, nobody expected that these experiments were going to be a financial success in themselves, because it is impossible for one to get at once the right kind of chickens to make a success of the system of fattening. The first year it is likely to be a comparative failure. The next year they get a better class of chickens, and year by year the financial results are more favourable. With reference to the industry In my own town, I remember the difficulty we had in selling eggs years ago- say in 1893, Chickens were bought at 5 cents per pound, and we were glad to get rid of them at that price. The difficulty was to sell them. Now, the thing is changed, and chickens are readily sold at good prices. The same was true of eggs. In 1893 we bought them and sold them at S cents per dozen. Allow me to give you one little incident with reference to the eggs : and I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will pass it over to the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor). In 1893 I was purchasing thousands and thousands of dozens of eggs at 8 cehts a dozen. A farmer came to my store with a basket of eggs and asked me what I would give him. I said : ' The best

I can do is 8 cents a dozen. I>o you see j those cases outside ? I have just sold them at 7$ cents a dozen-I am losing a quarter of a cent on every dozen.' ' Well,' he said,
* what are the farmers of this country going to do ? We cannot raise eggs at that price. We will have to go to the other side, or do something else. The fact is that that price will not pay for the wear and tear of the hens.' Now, let me show you how all this is changed. And, in order to show, I will read a few lines from a circular I received the other day from Montreal:
Montreal, June 14th.
Dear Sir,-We will give you 14 cents for all the fresh eggs you can ship this week.
How does that compare with 8 cents a dozen in the old Conservative days ? I think that the farmers realize that they are living under a different administration, and will give credit to whom credit is due. Now,
1	wish to say a word with reference to the fattening of chickens.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: What do you pay for eggs ?

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
We pay 15 cents a dozen, and cannot get enough of them at that. Now, let me read an extract from the Renfrew ' Mercury ' of February 14th, 1902-this date being just a short time after the chicken fattening station had been established in Renfrew. And let me call your attention to the fact, and to ask you to bear it in mind, that the person who gives the information to the Renfrew 1 Mercury ' is Mr. David Muirhead, a leading Conservative in our town, and president of the Farmers' Institute :
An Admaston farmer resolved to make a test -to see if in farm practice there was really any profit in fattening chickens on the plan followed at the government's experimental station here a short time ago. So he took 30 ordinary chickens-not. at all large ones-and fed them on oats and barley, mixed with low grade flour-for five weeks, and then sent 24 of them off to a Montreal commission merchant whose name was one of several which had been furnished him by Mr. F. C. Hare, the government's demonstrator. He received answer that the 24 fowl had weighed 158 pounds, and remittance was made -for them at the rate of 11 cents (eleven) cents a pound in Montreal. The ex-pressage cost the Admaston farmer 80 cents per 100 pounds, so that he received $10.20 per 100 pounds net for his fowl. The fowl were kept confined in coops, were fed twice a day, and in the five weeks the thirty ate 8 bushels of oats,
2	bushels of barley, and 100 pounds of low-grade (unsaleable) flour with just enough skim-milk added to make the food moist. Water to drink and gravel to peck were supplied. The farmer was so well pleased with the result of his experiment, that he will fatten more chickens next year. He knows nothing that pays better for the amount of labour involved. The merchant to whom he sold rather took his breath away by writing that if he could supply broilers weighing II or 2 pounds in April or May, he would get 45 cents a pound for them.
I wish to place before the House account sales of the eggs that were shipped from my town last winter. I have here an invoice of eggs which were sold to Bate & Co., in Ottawa :
February 10, 12 dozen fresh eggs at 40 cents, $4.80.
How does that compare with your eight cents under the Conservative rule ?
February 17, 12 dozen fresh eggs at 40 cents, $4.80.
February 19, 12 dozen fresh eggs at 40 cents, $4.80.
February 26, 24 dozen fresh eggs at 40 cents, $9.60.
March 4, 24 dozen fresh eggs at 35 cents, $8.40.
March 11, 24 dozen fresh eggs at 35 cents, $8.40. a total of $40.80.
This will show you whether there is money in raising eggs if you do it properly.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Might I ask what change has been brought about by this government to cause the price of eggs to go up ?

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: They have got a lot of suckers around.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
They are teaching the people how to raise the eggs, and to have them for market at a proper time. They also have helped to obtain a market for them. We are getting a home market now and we are also getting more for anything sent abroad than we got before. I have here some invoices of eggs sent to Walter Paul, of Montreal. Here is one :
January 25, 9 dozen eggs at 40 cents, $3.60.
January 25, 3 dozen eggs, small, at 30 cents, 90 cents.
This shows you the discrimination there is now. In the old days there was not this discrimination.
I have here also an invoice for eggs shipped to Mr. Henry Gatehouse, of Montreal :
January 12, 24 dozen eggs at 30 cents, $7.20.
I have others which show about the same rates.
I have here also invoices of chickens sent to Mr. Gatehouse.
Here is one :
October 1, 2 coops chickens, 60 - 66=126 at 12 cents, $15.12.
That certainly^, is better that the 5 cents a pound which we got in the old days.
Here is another :
March, 30, 50 pounds fowl at 9 cents a pound, $4.50.
There were 6 fowls in this and they netted him 75 cents each.
Here is another one :
October 30, 139 pounds chickens at 10 cents a pound, $13.90.
There were 20 chickens in this lot so that they netted him 70 cents each. Surely this

ought to prove that the lessons which have been given to the farmers in our section of the country have been productive of much good. If any other evidence is necessary to prove that the farmers are doing better than they did we can find it in the export of farm produce which is now being made. In 1896 we exported only $50,000,000 worth of farm products whereas last year we exported no less than $114,000,000. In 1896 we sent in round numbers only $14,000,000 worth of cheese, whereas last year we sent out $25,000,000 worth. Surely this shows that this country is progressing and that the farmers are moving onward.
A good deal of fault has been .found with regard to the Minister of Agriculture himself, the statetnent being made that he is not a proper man to fill that position. I would like to show you how an outsider regards the present Minister of Agriculture. Here is a letter which was published in the Renfrew ' Mercury.' The letter was written from Riverside, California, on March 31, 1904. I need not read the first part of the letter but I shall quote this portion which refers to the Minister of Agriculture :
In an agricultural way you lave gained enormously over this country. Speaking recently with one of the ablest men who are taking care of our agricultural and horticultural interests at Washington I was really pleased to have him say that the Department of Agriculture in Canada was far in advance of that in this country.
Surely this does not look much as if we had inefficient men at the head of affairs here. I am proud to say, I am proud to know that the farmers of this country are progressing and when the day comes for the farmers to give their verdict I have no doubt in my own mind that the verdict will be that the present government shall be returned and that the Minister of Agriculture will be maintained in his position. Then the farmers will go on progressing at the same rate as they have done for the last six or seven years.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I would not have taken any part in this discussion were it not that a remark made by the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) caused me to look at the record of that chicken fattening station of which he seems to feel so proud, and criticism of which he seems to think would be of no assistance to his opponents in his own riding. I think it is a function of the government to make experiments and we do not expect the result of the experiments in each case to be a profit, but in this experimental station at Holmesville-and I believe the same thing is true of all the chicken fattening stations-the proceeds of the sales do not pay for the feed and the cost of the chickens bought, and surely the feed cannot be charged up to experimenting. Surely if they are feeding these chickens on new improved scientific principles they should be able to sell the chickens for
the amount which the feed cost and the cost of the purchased chickens, especially when we are informed that they are sold at an advanced price, at a price 2 to 4 cents more than the ordinary price. In connection with this Holmesville fattening station the only item outside of feed and purchased fowls which I will take into account are $13.40 for coal oil and $28.40 for plucking the chickens. There are $9.85 for cold storage and all the rest is for feed and the cost of the chickens, making the total cost $902.85. In this not a single dollar is taken into account for labour, but no farmer or any one else could fatten chickens without some labour.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: In the Auditor General's Report for last year, the hon. member will find that there is an expenditure of over $1,000 for buildings.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I am not taking one single cent of that into account. If the hon. gentleman had listened he would have heard me state that I did not take into account a single cent except the cost of chickens and the feed. I did not count in a cent for labour or for sundries although there is an item of $100 charged for sundries. The total cost for feed, chickens bought and the three small items mentioned about which there can be do difference of opinion as to the propriety of the charge is $902.85 and the receipts from the sales last year were $564.57 leaving a deficit of $338.28, although we are counting nothing but the cost of the feed and the chickens themselves and the minor items before mentioned.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.

speechtext: The work which was done did not result in any benefit at ail because the tests were not successful in locating any oil in paying quantities. My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) is familiar, no doubt, with the oil business, and he will probably agree with me that the oil prospector is the man who is going to find the oil-the man who makes a business of prospecting is more likely to find it than the scientific officer of the geological survey. The work of the survey, so far as that is concerned, is more properly done by giving information as to the locality in which the geological deposits are of such a character that oil may he looked for there with some probability of finding it. But as to putting down test holes and carrying on the practical work of prospecting for oil, experience shows that we had better leave that to the prospector. As I said, we were not successful in the test holes put down though these experiments cost a good deal of money. Under our Northwest land regulations we encourage the making of tests for oil, and a number of commercial companies are carrying on testing operations at the present time, some of them with a degree of success. In one or two locations there are wells which, though not very productive, yield oil in paying quantities.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: In regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for East Lambton, (Mr. Armstrong) as I happen to represent the part of the country to which he refers I may be allowed a word or two. I do not wish to take the position of asking or demanding special expenditures in that part of the country. At the same time, if it should be the will of parliament to authorize an expenditure for boring for oil in that part of the country, certainly the project would have my most hearty approval. As to the experiments that have been made, I have a little crow to pick with the geological survey in that matter, and will take this opportunity of placing the facts before the committee. It is a number of years now since' the late government thought fit to institute explorations for oil in that part of the country. They put down a well at Athabasca Landing, 100 miles north of Edmonton, where there was no sign of oil. They found none. They put down another well at Victoria, 80 miles northeast, where there is not and never was-never was reported to be-any sign of oil. They did not find any. They also put down a well at Pelican Rapids, down the Athabasca about 120 miles below the landing where there has always been a flow of natural gas. They struck a very heavy flow of natural gas, but so far as I am aware no oil, and they suspended operations. The machinery having been transported 120 miles down the river by flatboat, I take it that the government believed that it would cost more to take care of machinery there than it was worth, and that if they undertook to bring it out it would cost more than it would be worth when brought out. Myqriarrel with the Geological Department is this-that they bored three wells where there was no sign of oil and where nobody suggested that there was a sign of oil. They arrived at the conclusion that they^ should bore there because of some theo-' ry of the director of the survey. They refused to bore for oil where there were surface indications of oil-they could not be induced to bore there. What I want to suggest to the minister is that if, the House being in generous mood as it seems to be, provides the money for further oil boring operations and the government undertake the work, the boring should be done where there are indications of oil, and not where there are no such indications. *

speechtext: I do not ask them and I do not intend to.

speechtext: That is a good thing for the hon. gentleman's constituents to know. I believe that we do not spend sufficient money on the Geological Survey. The opening of even one mine would more than bring back to the country the amount of money expended in this way.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: 'Purchasing specimens,' what does that mean ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
That refers to some small purchases from time to time of some small specimens of rocks which may be in the possession of private individuals. The department may require them for examination or may not have a sample of that parti-Mr. OLIVER.
cular variety. The amounts paid are very trifling.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I thought this was to purchase specimens for exhibition. You usually use a portion of your vote every year .lor the purpose of supplying specimens to schools and collegiate institutes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I should have added that in some cases where very fine geological specimens are in the hands of private individuals and the officers of the survey think they would be of value for the permanent museum they are purchased. Of course, the amounts that are paid are comparatively small. As to the cabinets of minerals that are sent to the schools they are not purchased. They are collected by the field officers. They make these collections for school purposes out of the surplus collection that they make in the course of their work in the field.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I see an item of $260.03 for postage paid to the Ottawa post office. I understood that the reports were sent out free of postage. Perhaps I am wrong on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I presume that that is for postage for letters sent to foreign countries that have to be paid for.
Geological Survey-for special explorations and surveys in British Columbia and the Yukon and the publication of reports and maps thereon, $19,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: This is a new item.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I gave the hon. gentleman the particulars as to that work.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: When ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: That is in the list I read.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman gave them, I have no remembrance of it. He gave a statement of the general work that was to be done in the different localities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: That included the work in British Columbia. There is no special reason why this should have been-put in a special item.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Why do you put it in a separate item ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
The ordinary vote is $60,000 but the director, after the first list had been made up, obtained my sanction for doing additional work in British Columbia and for the submission of the amount of money that was required to do that additional work. The amount is $10,000 and a further item is put in for it.
Geological Survey-to provide for plotting and compiling of surveys, plans, maps, and utilizing field notes, &c., $5,566.25.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
The hon. Minister of Interior (Mr. Sifton) moves to amend the item by adding the following

Salaries, greater than $500 per annum may be paid from this vote, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: What is the explanation of that ? There is nothing about salaries in this item.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: If the director requires to call in an expert for a short period he will have to pay him whatever his services are worth, or whatever the person who is employed demands and the director thinks a fair amount. These services are only of a temporary character and it amounts to very iittle, but the terms of the Civil Service Act are such that he could not pay a man under such circumstances more than $500. _ He would have to go in as a clerk at $500 a year, and in order to enable the director to employ persons of special capabilities for a short time this is put in. As an illustration, I may say that one of the officers lately was making a special investigation into the question of nickel, and there was some metallurgical work thait was required. As they did not have an officer in the survey to do it, they had to employ somebody temporarily, and they secured the services of a gentleman from McGill College, who was paid, I think, $100 a month.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I would like to ask the bon. minister whether there is anything in this item, No. 198, for any further explorations in the Peace River district?

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. minister if he has brought down that report that he promised in regard to Mr. Stewart ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY INTER-IMPERIAL PREFERENTIAL TRADE-DISMISSAL OF LORD DUNDONALD.
speechtext:
I will bring it down tomorrow.
Some resolutions reported.

speechtext: There may be some Bills at the earlier stage, and in supply the estimates of the Prime Minister, the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture, and in the afternoon the estimates of the Minister of the Interior will probably be resumed.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
What Bills ?
Mr. FIELDING The Prime Minister did not state.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I had an understanding with the Minister of the Interior that he would go on with the immigration estimates immediately after the Bills. If we get into the other estimates we cannot tall when they will be reached.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would like to ask if it is the intention to have an item of that character placed in the estimates ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I cannot say till I see the report of the committee.
To pay for assay apparatus and chemicals, metallurgical, petrographical, library and clerical assistance (salaries greater than $500 per annum may be paid from this vote, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act), $6,300.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: How is it that you have to put salaries in here again?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: The remarks I made a short time ago apply to that.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I would like to know if Mr. J. B. Lindsay has any land leased in townships 8 and 9 and ranges 5 and 6, west of the 4th meridian. I shall be glad to furnish the hon. minister with a short note I have here if he would be good enough to furnish the information. What I want to know is how many acres of grazing lands, with the date and price, have been leased to Mr. J. B. Lindsay, in townships 8 and 9, range 6, west of 4th meridian, or in township 8, range 5, west of 4th meridian, and what homestead entries have been made in township 8, range 5, west of 4th meridian.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman send the memorandum down ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: The Minister of the Interior tells me that he will be ready to go on with his estimates immediately upon supply being moved, so that the Interior estimates will have priority.
